blocks.kotobagaki: 四十三　父母ソノ兒子ノ夙達ヲ望ベカラザル事
blocks.text: 龜ハ、行歩ノ最モ遲キモノナリ、然𪜈當然ノ道ヲ勉メテ行クトキハ、敏速ニシテ當然ノ道ヲ行ザル生類ト先ヲ爭ヒ、却テ勝ヲ奏スベシ、故ニ少年ノ人、但能勤勉ナレバ、遲鈍ナルヲ患ベカラズ、然ノミナラズ、事ノ敏速ナルハ、時トシテ弊害トナルヿアリ、譬バ童子ノ速ニ學課ヲ記憶スルモノハ、ソノ忘却スルヿマタ速カナルが如シ、蓋シ事ヲ做ニ敏速ナル童子ハ、勤勉堅忍ノ性ヲ養ヒ成ヿ能ズ、遲鈍ナル少年ハ、自ラコノ性ヲ造リ出ザルヿヲ得ズ、コノ勤勉恒耐ノ性ハ、實ニ衆善百行ノ根基ニシテ、尤モ貴ビ重ンズベキモノナリ、大未曰ク、我が我レタル所以ノモノハ、皆吾が自己ニ造リ成セルモノナリト、コノ言ヤ、世人各ソノ眞確ナルヲ覺ベシ、コノ編ヲ終ルニ臨ミ、要領ヲ提グベシ、凡ソ人、少年ノ時、學校ニ在テ、敎師ヨリ受タル敎養ノ益ハ、甚ダ少ク、大人トナリシ後、自己ニ勤勉學習シタル脩養ノ益ハ、甚ダ多シ、サレバ、父母タルモノ、ソノ兒子ノ才能夙ニ顯レ、早ク英華ヲ吐ヿヲ、急ニ見ト思ベカラズ、宜ク心ヲ着テ、兒子ヲ護守シ、久キヲ忍テ等侯シ、良善ノ表樣ヲ立テ、安靜ノ敎養ヲ爲シテ、ソレヲシテ課業ヲ勉シムベシ、コレヨリ以上ハ、天命ニ信スベキナリ、且父母タルモノハ、童子ヲシテ、自由ニ身體ヲ運動シ、康健ナラシメ、コレニ繼デ、ソレヲシテ自ラ脩ムルノ道途ニ入ラシメ、勉强恒耐ノ慣習ヲ長ゼシムベシ、然トキハ、童子生長スルニ隨ヒ、自脩ルノ志氣次第ニ壯盛ナルヿヲ得ベキナリ、
blocks.genbun:
The tortoise in the right road will beat a racer in the wrong. It matters not though a youth be slow, if he be but diligent. Quickness of parts may even prove a defect, inasmuch as the boy who learns readily will often forget as readily; and also because he finds no need of cultivating that quality of application and perseverance which the slower youth is compelled to exercise, and which proves so valuable an element in the formation of every character. Davy said “What I am I have made myself;” and the same holds true universally.
To conclude: the best culture is not obtained from teachers when at school or college, so much as by our own diligent self-education when we have become men. Hence parents need not be in too great haste to see their children’s talents forced into bloom. Let them watch and wait patiently, letting good example and quiet training do their work, and leave the rest to Providence. Let them see to it that the youth is provided, by free exercise of his bodily powers, with a full stock of physical health; set him fairly on the road of self-culture; carefully train his habits of application and perseverance; and as he grows older, if the right stuff be in him, he will be enabled vigorously and effectively to cultivate himself.

chu.n: 原文にある「本人の中にしかるべき素質があるならば」という条件は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 義律曰、人身ハ、縊殺セラルベシ、行狀ハ、縊殺セラルベカラズ、蓋シ人ソノ自知ル良心ノ中ニ滅亡スベカラザル生命ヲ有リ、
blocks.genbun:
“Ever their phantoms rise before us, Our loftier brothers, but one in blood; By bed and table they lord it o’er us, With looks of beauty and words of good.”—John Sterling.
“Children may be strangled, but Deeds never; they have an indestructible life, both in and out of our consciousness.”—George Eliot.

chu.n: 原書はこの前に、ジョン・スターリングの詩の四行を題辞として置く（段落 1）。中村の訳にはない。義律はジョージ・エリオット。原文は「子どもは絞め殺せるが、行いは絞め殺せない」で、行いには「われわれの意識の内でも外でも」滅びない命がある、という。中村は「子ども」を「人身」、「意識の内でも外でも」を「自知ル良心ノ中ニ」と訳している

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 托馬士〇阿弗〇馬爾墨士坂禮曰、今生ニ於テ、凡ソ人ノ行爲ハ、後事相繫屬スル長久ノ鏈ノ端首トナラザルモノナシ、ソノ長久ナル末梢ノ光景ハ、肉眼ノ能達スルトコロニ非ズ、

ruby.a: 托馬士〇阿弗〇馬爾墨士坂禮
ruby.r: トマスオフマルメスベレイ

blocks.genbun: “There is no action of man in this life, which is not the beginning of so long a chain of consequences, as that no human providence is high enough to give us a prospect to the end.”—Thomas of Malmesbury.

chu.a: 肉眼ノ能達スルトコロニ非ズ
chu.n: 原文は「人間のどんな先見も、その終わりまでを見晴らせるほど高くはない」

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 一　家裡ノ敎化最モ緊要ナル事、并ニ家國同一ナル事
blocks.text: 好儀範ハ、舌ナクシテ甚ダ勢力アルノ敎師ト稱スベシ、蓋シ人生實際ノ學問ハ、行爲ノ上ニ在リ、故ニ好儀範ノ、人ヲ感移スルヿ、言語ノ比スベキニ非ズ、敎訓ノ善ナルモノハ、固ヨリ斤兩アリテ重ズベシ、然𪜈儀範ノ善モノアリテ、コレニ伴ハザレバ、ソノ人ニ入ルヿ必ズ深カラズ、命令訓敕ハ、人生ノ行ベキ道路ヲ指示スニ過ズ、好表樣ヲ立ル人ハ、コレト親炙シ附近スルモノヲシテ、自ラ習慣シテコレト共ニ化セシムルナリ、サレバ、常言ニ、「我が言フ如ニ爲ベシ、我が爲ス如クニ爲ヿ勿レ」ト云ルハ正道ニ反シテ行ルベカラザルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: EXAMPLE is one of the most potent of instructors, though it teaches without a tongue. It is the practical school of mankind, working by action, which is always more forcible than words. Precept may point to us the way, but it is silent continuous example, conveyed to us by habits, and living with us in fact, that carries us along. Good advice has its weight: but without the accompaniment of a good example it is of comparatively small influence; and it will be found that the common saying of “Do as I say, not as I do,” is usually reversed in the actual experience of life.

chu.a: 正道ニ反シテ行ルベカラザルヿナリ
chu.n: 原文は、このことわざは実際の暮らしではふつう逆になる（人は言われたとおりにではなく、されたとおりにする）、という意味

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 凡ソ人、目見ニ由リテ智識ヲ得ルヿ、耳聞ニ比スレバ多シ、眞實ニ觀覽シテ證知スルヿハ、特ニ讀ミ聞モノニ比スレバ、ソノ心ニ覺感スルコト、遙ニ深シトス、就中兒童ハ、眼目ヲ以テ知識ノ門戶ト爲ス、凡ソノ見ルトコロノ事ハ、知ズ覺ズ、自ラコレヲ視傚モノナリ、故ニ兒童ハ己ノ傍ニ圍繞シ共ニ居トコロノ人ノ表樣ニ、自ラ似ルヿ、恰モ虫ノ色、ソノ食フ所ノ葉ノ色ニ似ルが如シ、サレバ、家裡ノ敎養ハ、最モ切要ナルモノニシテ、决シテ忽ニスベカラズ、抑モ鄕塾府學ニテ敎ルトコロ、固ヨリソノ功効ナシト云ベカラズ、然𪜈、家裡ニ於テ立ルトコロノ好儀範ノ感化ニハ及ベクモアラズ、家中ノ儀範コソ、實ニ後來男女ノ品行ヲ鎔鑄スル基本ナレ、
blocks.genbun: All persons are more or less apt to learn through the eye rather than the ear; and, whatever is seen in fact, makes a far deeper impression than anything that is merely read or heard. This is especially the case in early youth, when the eye is the chief inlet of knowledge. Whatever children see they unconsciously imitate. They insensibly come to resemble those who are about them—as insects take the colour of the leaves they feed on. Hence the vast importance of domestic training. For whatever may be the efficiency of schools, the examples set in our Homes must always be of vastly greater influence in forming the characters of our future men and women.

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 夫レ流動物ノ凝結シテ堅硬ノ物ニ化スルヤ、或ハ三角、或ハ四角ソノ他種々ノ形狀アリ、各ソノ性質ニ隨ヒ、各樣ノ形ヲ現ゼリ、ソノ如ク、風俗ノ情形ハ家風ノ聚合スルモノニシテ邦國ノ體格ハ家範ノ團結スルモノナリ、蓋シ家ハ、邦國ノ核仁ナリ、家ニ在テ、爲トコロノモノ、外ニ發出シテ、風俗トナリ、格言法語トナル、故ニ一家ノ治法ハ、即チ邦國ノ治法、ソノ正邪純駁、二致ナシ、特ニ大小ノ異ナルアルノミ、各家ノ私論ハ即闔國ノ公論、ソノ曲直高下、二端ナシ、特ニ廣狹ノ異アルノミ、蓋シ邦國ハ、コノ家中ノ乳養ニ由テ生長シ、仁善ヲ行ヒ一世ヲ利益スル人ハ、火爐ノ邊ヨリ顯レ出ヅ、培克曰、人各ソノ小數ノ夥伴ヲ愛スルヿハ、邦國公同親愛ノ萌芽〔始ト云フが如シ〕ナリト、誠ニコノ言ノ如ク、家裡ノ親愛ハ、環心ノ小點ノ如ク、コレヨリシテ、仁恕ノ周圍、次第ニ廣ク、慈愛ノ圈圓、愈大ニシテ、全地球ヲ懷抱スルニ至ベシ、諺ニ曰、慈悲喜捨ハ、家ヨリ始ト、然バ家ニ止ルベカラズシテ、必ズ邦國天下ニ推シ及スベキヿヲ知ルベシ、
notes: 培克享保十三年生寛政九年沒以文章名
blocks.genbun: The Home is the crystal of society—the nucleus of national character; and from that source, be it pure or tainted, issue the habits, principles and maxims, which govern public as well as private life. The nation comes from the nursery. Public opinion itself is for the most part the outgrowth of the home; and the best philanthropy comes from the fireside. “To love the little platoon we belong to in society,” says Burke, “is the germ of all public affections.” From this little central spot, the human sympathies may extend in an ever widening circle, until the world is embraced; for, though true philanthropy, like charity, begins at home, assuredly it does not end there.

chu.a: 夫レ流動物ノ凝結シテ
chu.n: 原文は「家庭は社会の結晶である」の一句。結晶がさまざまな形をとるという説明は、中村が加えたもの
一家の治め方と国の治め方、家々の私論と国の公論を対にして述べる所は、中村が言葉を足して敷衍したもの。原文は、家庭から出る習慣・主義・格言が公の生活も私の生活も治める、世論もおおかたは家庭から育つ、と短く言う

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 二　父母ノ儀範
blocks.text: 品行儀範ハ、縱ヒ極テ瑣細ナル事ト雖モ、決シテ輕シ忽ニスベカラズ、何ニトナレバ、コノ事、常ニ他人ノ行狀ニ關係シ、善惡トモニ他人ニ分チ與ヿナリ、サレバ父母ノ爲シ擧動ハ、ソノ子必ズ再三コレヲ行モノニシテ、就中父母ノ每日言行ニ顯ルル、仁愛ノ事、循守スル所ノ規矩、勤勉ノ事、及自ラ其身ヲ謹修ル事、凡ソカクノ如モノハ、其子久後ニ至𪜈、自ラ心目ノ間ニ在テ忘ベカラズ、耳ヨリ聞ルモノハ、盡ク忘却スル後ト雖𪜈、コノ目ニテ習慣セシヿハ、憶ヒ出シテ、コレニ倣ント思フ志、マタ萌生ス、故ニ昔賢常ニソノ子ノ事ヲ稱シテ、將來ノ我ト云モノアリ、且父母ノ獨自默然トシテ爲トコロノ行ト雖𪜈、父母ノ自ラ省知セザル偶然ノ容色ト雖𪜈、往々ソノ兒子ノ心中ニ印識シ、終身磨滅セザルヿアリ、况ヤ父母ノ善良ナル心術、端正ナル行爲ハ、ソノ兒子ノ記臆ニ留ルヿ、殊ニ深トス、故ニ年長ズルノ後、或ハ汚穢ナル想念ニ陷リ、卑陋ナル行狀ニ沈ヿアリトモ、中夜夢醒ル時、忽チ父母ノ平生ヲ思ヒ起ス時ハ、怵然トシテ感悔シ、惡念拭が如ク消除シ、行狀頓ニ善ニ改マルヿアリ、コレヲ以テ、父母ノ儀範、ソノ感化ノ遠ニ及ヿヲ見ベシ、
blocks.genbun: Example in conduct, therefore, even in apparently trivial matters, is of no light moment, inasmuch as it is constantly becoming inwoven with the lives of others, and contributing to form their natures for better or for worse. The characters of parents are thus constantly repeated in their children; and the acts of affection, discipline, industry, and self-control, which they daily exemplify, live and act when all else which may have been learned through the ear has long been forgotten. Hence a wise man was accustomed to speak of his children as his “future state.” Even the mute action and unconscious look of a parent may give a stamp to the character which is never effaced; and who can tell how much evil act has been stayed by the thought of some good parent, whose memory their children may not sully by the commission of an unworthy deed, or the indulgence of an impure thought?

chu.n: 原文は「善い親を思うことで、どれほど多くの悪い行いが食い止められてきたか、だれに分かろう」という問いかけ。夜中に夢から覚めて父母を思い起こす、という場面は中村が加えたもの

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 三　物斯的、勃古斯敦等、ソノ母ニ感化セラレシ事
blocks.text: 極テ瑣細ナル事ト雖𪜈、人生ノ品行ヲ造リ出ス最要ノ感化トナルヿアリ、サレバ、物斯的ハ、吾母ノ一親嘴、我ヲシテ畫工トナラシメタリト云リ、蓋シ父母ノ爲ル瑣小ノ事ニテモ、ソノ兒子後來福運ノ基トナルヿ、カクノ如シ、豈忽ニスベケンヤ、勃古斯敦、顯達ノ後、ソノ品行、衆人ノ模楷ト仰ルヽ時、嘗テ其母ニ書ヲ贈テ曰、吾他人ノ爲ニ心力ヲ盡シテ辭セザルヿハ、母君平日ノ持論定見、吾幼時ノ心中ニ種子ヲ播タルモノヽ現出ル效驗ナリト云リ、勃古斯敦、マタソノ圃人普拉斯的ト云ルモノヨリ、觀感ノ益ヲ受シヿヲ、時々語リ、普拉斯的ハ、沒字漢ナリシガ、性質善良ニシテ、事理ニ通ジ、謀慮决斷ノ才アリ、勃氏少時コレト共ニ遊嬉シ、馬ニ乘リ、相歡愛セリ、後來勃氏普ヲ評シテ曰、普ノ尤モ敬重スベキモノハ、ソノ忠實ニシテ廉耻ノ節アルニ在リ、普吾母ノ家ニ在ザル時ト雖𪜈、決シテ一言タリ𪜈、吾母ノ許ザルヿヲ言ズ、一事タリ𪜈吾母ノ許ザルヿヲ爲ズ、ソノ忠實ノ行、極テ高ク、且純正寛大ナル識見ヲ以テ、吾輩少年ノ心ニ滿タリ、昔賢設涅加、細設洛ノ文集ノ中ニ見エタル、純正寛大ナル議論ト雖𪜈、コレニ過ズ、實ニ普ハ吾最初ノ敎師ナリ、マタ吾最善ノ敎師ナリト云シトナリ、
blocks.genbun: The veriest trifles thus become of importance in influencing the characters of men. “A kiss from my mother,” said West, “made me a painter.” It is on the direction of such seeming trifles when children that the future happiness and success of men mainly depend. Fowell Buxton, when occupying an eminent and influential station in life, wrote to his mother, “I constantly feel, especially in action and exertion for others, the effects of principles early implanted by you in my mind.” Buxton was also accustomed to remember with gratitude the obligations which he owed to an illiterate man, a gamekeeper, named Abraham Plastow, with whom he played, and rode, and sported—a man who could neither read nor write, but was full of natural good sense and mother-wit. “What made him particularly valuable,” says Buxton, “were his principles of integrity and honour. He never said or did a thing in the absence of my mother of which she would have disapproved. He always held up the highest standard of integrity, and filled our youthful minds with sentiments as pure and as generous as could be found in the writings of Seneca or Cicero. Such was my first instructor, and, I must add, my best.”

chu.n: 原文は「エイブラハム・プラストーという名の、読み書きのできない猟場番」。プラストーとは、遊び、馬に乗り、狩りをしたとある

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 勞爾德〔爵名〕闌第爾、ソノ母ノ好儀範ヲ回憶シ、コレヲ贊美シテ曰、全地球ヲ天平ノ此ノ端ニ懸ケ、吾母ヲ天平ノ彼ノ端ニ懸タランニハ、全地球必ズ天平ヲ踢ベシ、〔全地球輕ク吾母重ルベシト云フ義〕ト云リ、
blocks.genbun: Lord Langdale, looking back upon the admirable example set him by his mother, declared, “If the whole world were put into one scale, and my mother into the other, the world would kick the beam.”

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 夫人悉金墨爾。便寧克老年ノ後、常ニソノ母ノ德行、能ク朋友會社ヲ風動セシヿヲ語リ、ソノ母一房ニ入トキハ、ソノ坐ニ會スル諸人轉ジテ高尙ナル談話トナルヿ、恰モ室中ノ濁氣ヲ除去テ、穆如タル清風ヲ以テ、コレニ滿ルが如シ、一坐ノ人ヲ觀ルニ、氣息更ニ寛舒ナルが如ク、容貌更ニ竪起スル如キヲ覺タリ、又曰、予吾母ノ面前ニ在シトキハ、自ラ變化シテ別人ト成シト云リ、蓋シ人常ニ德善ノ風氣ヲ呼吸スルヿハ、德善ノ志氣、自ラ健康ナルヲ得ベシ、故ニ父母毎日兒子ノ眼前ニ在テ行トコロノモノ、ソノ兒子ヲ風動感移スルヿ、甚ダ大ナレバ、父母タルモノ自ラソノ身ヲ修ルコソ、兒子ヲ敎育スル最要ナルベケレ、サレバ、世ノ父母ヲ戒ル法言、タヾ二字ヲ以テ包括スベシ、曰イムプルーヴザイセルフ〔汝自ラ修善セヨ〕、
blocks.genbun: Mrs. Schimmel Penninck, in her old age, was accustomed to call to mind the personal influence exercised by her mother upon the society amidst which she moved. When she entered a room it had the effect of immediately raising the tone of the conversation, and as if purifying the moral atmosphere—all seeming to breathe more freely, and stand more erectly. “In her presence,” says the daughter, “I became for the time transformed into another person.” So much does she moral health depend upon the moral atmosphere that is breathed, and so great is the influence daily exercised by parents over their children by living a life before their eyes, that perhaps the best system of parental instruction might be summed up in these two words: “Improve thyself.”

chu.a: 德善ノ志氣、自ラ健康ナルヲ得ベシ
chu.n: 原書の電子テキストは「So much does she moral health depend」とするが、she は the の誤植。「道徳の健康は、呼吸する道徳の空気にそれほど左右される」の意に直して訳した

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 四　人ノ言行將來ト必ズ相關ル事
blocks.text: 人一言一行ト雖𪜈、決シテ一時ニ止ルモノニ非ズ、必ズコレニ從フ關係ノ事アリテ相續キ、將來ノ遠ニ傳リ及ブモノニテ、ソノ結尾ハ、人ノ决シテ踪跡スル能ザルヿナリ、コレヲ思ベ、凛然トシテ恐懼ノ心生ズルヲ覺ベシ、蓋人ニハ、必ソノ色アリテ、他人ニ其色ヲ分チ與ヘ、ソノ己ト交ル人ヲシテ、知ズ覺ズ、己ニ感移セシムルモノナリ、善言善行ハ、縱自ソノ果實ヲ結ヲ見ザルヿアリ𪜈、切ニコノ世ニ永ク留テ死セザルベシ、獨此ノミナラズ、惡言惡行モ亦然リ、愼ザルベケンヤ、又一種ノ人、善ヲモ行ズ、惡ヲモ爲ザルモノアリ、惡人ヨリハ勝ベケレ𪜈、畢竟賤ムベクシテ取ニ足ズ、抑モ人ノ精神死セズ、故ニ已ニ死セルモノモ、吾輩ト共ニ生キ、共ニ行歩スルヿナリ、垤士禮立、甞テ格伯田ノ死セシ時、百姓議院ニ於テ述シ言辭、巧妙ニシテ且眞確ナリ、ソノ言ニ曰、格伯田ノ如キ人ハ、縱ヒ今コヽニ在ズト雖𪜈、ナホコノ議院ノ官員ニ列セリ、カクノ如キ人ハ、死亡ノ事ニ關ラズ、民委官ヲ選ブ人ノ變化ニ拘ラズ、マタ時代ノ推遷ニ關ザルモノナリト云リ、

ruby.r: メムベアヲヴパーリメント

blocks.genbun: There is something solemn and awful in the thought that there is not an act done or a word uttered by a human being but carries with it a train of consequences, the end of which we may never trace. Not one but, to a certain extent, gives a colour to our life, and insensibly influences the lives of those about us. The good deed or word will live, even though we may not see it fructify, but so will the bad; and no person is so insignificant as to be sure that his example will not do good on the one hand, or evil on the other. The spirits of men do not die: they still live and walk abroad among us. It was a fine and a true thought uttered by Mr. Disraeli in the House of Commons on the death of Richard Cobden, that “he was one of those men who, though not present, were still members of that House, who were independent of dissolutions, of the caprices of constituencies, and even of the course of time.”

chu.n: 原文は「自分の手本が一方で善を、他方で悪をなすことはないと言い切れるほど、取るに足りない人はいない」。善も悪もしない人を卑しむ、という中村の訳は原文と違う
原文の dissolutions は議会の解散のこと。「解散にも、選挙区の気まぐれにも、時の流れにさえも左右されない」と言う

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 五　人ノ言行永ク死セザル事
blocks.text: 人、來世ニ於テ、靈魂死セザルノミナラズ、コノ世界ニ於テモ、亦死セズ滅セザル本質ヲ存セリ、人ハ宇宙ノ間ニアリテ、獨立モノニ非ス、互ニ相依賴シ關係スルモノヽ一分ナリ、而人ノ種々ナル事業ニ賴テ、人類一統ノ幸福ヲ、或ハ增シ、或ハ減シ、永遠無疆ニ及ヿナリ、現在ノ人世ハ、過去ヨリ根ヲ發ス、吾等先祖ノ言行儀範、實ニ吾等ヲ感化鎔鑄スルヿ、時代隔ト雖𪜈、尙新ナルが如シ、コノ理ヲ推ベ、吾等今世ニ在テ、每日行トコロノモノ、亦將來ノ景象ヲ甄陶シ、後世ノ風格ヲ模造スルモノトナルベシ、蓋シ今日ノ人ハ、數百年ノ前ヨリ、培養ヲ受タルモノヽ成熟セル菓實ナリ、而ソノ言行儀範、磁石氣ノ流行スルが如ク、上ハ千載ノ前ニ接シ、下ハ千載ノ後ニ達ス、故ニ人死シテ、ソノ身體消散シ、土ト化シ、氣ニ雜ルト雖𪜈、ソノ善惡ノ言行ハ、死セズ、散セズ、各ソノ種類ニ隨テ、將來ノ菓實ヲ結ビ、無疆ニ傳ルベシ、サレバ人ノ斯世ニ在ル、ソノ職任ノ重コト、幾何ゾヤ、ソノ關係ノ大ナルコト、幾何ゾヤ、コレヲ思ヘバ、慄然トシテ懼レ、慄然トシテ戒ザルヲ得ンヤ、
blocks.genbun: There is, indeed, an essence of immortality in the life of man, even in this world. No individual in the universe stands alone; he is a component part of a system of mutual dependencies; and by his several acts he either increases or diminishes the sum of human good now and for ever. As the present is rooted in the past, and the lives and examples of our forefathers still to a great extent influence us, so are we by our daily acts contributing to form the condition and character of the future. Man is a fruit formed and ripened by the culture of all the foregoing centuries; and the living generation continues the magnetic current of action and example destined to bind the remotest past with the most distant future. No man’s acts die utterly; and though his body may resolve into dust and air, his good or his bad deeds will still be bringing forth fruit after their kind, and influencing future generations for all time to come. It is in this momentous and solemn fact that the great peril and responsibility of human existence lies.

chu.n: 「来世で霊魂が死なないだけでなく」は中村が加えたもの。原文は「この世にあってさえ、人の生涯には不死の本質がある」と言うだけ

chu.a: サレバ人ノ斯世ニ在ル
chu.n: 結びは、原文では「人が生きることの大きな危うさと責任は、この重大で厳かな事実の中にある」の一文。中村は言葉を重ねて訳している

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 六　拔倍籍言行不死ノ論文
blocks.text: 拔倍籍ノ文章ノ中ニ、コノ上ニ言ル意ヲ、切實ニ論ゼリ、曰今夫一人ノ身體、絲毫ノ分子ト雖𪜈、或ハ善或ハ惡ヲ以テ、ソノ中ニ沁入セリ、古聖賢ノ身ナリシ原質ノ一分ヲ、吾身ノ中ニ含ミ、ソノ時動作セシモノヲ保存シ、又百千ノ鄙夫凡流ノ身ナリシ原質ヲ滲合シ、ソノ時活動セシモノヲ貯ルヿナリ、又人ノ呼吸スル天空ノ氣ハ、廣大ナル書庫ナリ、ソノ紙頁ノ中ニ、開闢以來、コノ世ニ出タル人ノ口ヨリ發スル言語ヲ盡ク載タリ、耳ニ附テ密語セシヿト雖𪜈、漏ヿナク、コレヲ永世無窮ニ傳ルナリ、サレバ、億萬ノ人、誓言ノ果ザルモノ、約束ノ踐ザルモノ、空氣ノ中ニ往來搖盪シ、百代變ゼズ、萬世朽ルヿナク、ソノ人ノ信義ヲ缺タル憑證ヲ存シテ、永ク案ニ在リ、抑モ天空ノ氣、カクノ如ク、人類ノ言語意見ヲ錄スル史官ナレバ、圈圓ナル地球、渺漫タル洋海、亦タ何ゾ獨吾人ノ行實ヲ永遠ニ證スルモノニアラザルベキヤ、凡ソ動クヿハ、自然ニ由ト人力ニ由トヲ論ゼズ、苟モ宇宙間ニ、動ヿアレバ、ソノ痕跡決シテ消除セラルベカラズ、蓋シ天地開テ後、始テ兇殺ヲ行フ人アリシ時、造物主既ニコノ人ノ額ニ、ソノ罪ノ記號ヲ印シ、又律法ヲ設ケ、後來コノ罪ヲ犯セル人ヲ處シ玉ヘリ、コノ罪ヲ犯シ人、ソノ身死シ、ソレゝノ原質ニ歸リ、ソノ原質又化シテ他人ノ一分トナル𪜈、ソノ罪ヲ犯シ時、筋力ノ動タルモノ、ソノ原質ノ分子ニ黏連シテ、消滅セズ、コレト共ニ、他人ノ身內ニ移リ住スルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: Mr. Babbage has so powerfully expressed this idea in a noble passage in one of his writings that we here venture to quote his words: “Every atom,” he says, “impressed with good or ill, retains at once the motions which philosophers and sages have imparted to it, mixed and combined in ten thousand ways with all that is worthless and base; the air itself is one vast library, on whose pages are written for ever all that man has ever said or whispered. There, in their immutable but unerring characters, mixed with the earliest as well as the latest sighs of mortality, stand for ever recorded vows unredeemed, promises unfulfilled; perpetuating, in the united movements of each particle, the testimony of man’s changeful will. But, if the air we breathe is the never-failing historian of the sentiments we have uttered, earth, air, and ocean, are, in like manner, the eternal witnesses of the acts we have done; the same principle of the equality of action and reaction applies to them. No motion impressed by natural causes, or by human agency, is ever obliterated. . . . If the Almighty stamped on the brow of the first murderer the indelible and visible mark of his guilt, He has also established laws by which every succeeding criminal is not less irrevocably chained to the testimony of his crime; for every atom of his mortal frame, through whatever changes its severed particles may migrate, will still retain adhering to it, through every combination, some movement derived from that very muscular effort by which the crime itself was perpetrated.”

chu.a: 一人ノ身體、絲毫ノ分子
chu.n: 原文は人の体に限らず、あらゆる原子について言う。「哲学者や賢人が与えた運動を、価値のない卑しいあらゆるものと幾万通りにも混じり合わせて保っている」とあり、古聖賢の体であった原質がわが身に含まれる、という中村の訳は言い換えになっている
原文はこの前に「作用と反作用が等しいという同じ原理が、これらにも当てはまる」の一句を置く。中村の訳にはない。また原文はこの文のあとに省略のしるし（. . .）を置き、引用を途中で飛ばしている

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 七　極テ卑賤ナル人ノ言行亦風俗ニ關係ス
blocks.text: 人一言ヲ道ヒ、一事ヲ行ヒ、一言ヲ聞キ、一事ヲ證スル每ニ、必ズ感化風動スルモノアリテ、コレニ從ヒ、己が將來ノ生涯ニ色澤ヲ生ズルノミナラズ、子孫朋友ニ色澤ヲ與ヘ、廣ク他人ニ被リ、一體ノ風俗ニ推移ヿナリ、ソノ感化ノ踪跡ハ、尋求がタシト雖𪜈、ソノ萬世無窮ニ傳リ及ヿハ、確然トシテ疑ベカラズ、サレバ、人ノ好儀範ヲ立ルハ、ソノ勢力ノ大ナルヿ、如何ニゾヤ、默シテ人ヲ化シ、言ズシテ人ヲ敎ヘ、極貧極微ノ地位ニ居ル𪜈、每日コノ事ヲ行ヒ得ラルベシ、抑モ世ニ二種ノ人アリ、ソノ一ハ、默シテ他人ヲ敎化スル人ナリ、其一ハ、默シテ他人ニ敎化セラルヽ人ナリ、他人ヲ敎化スル人ヨリ貴ハナシ、酬銀ナキ敎化ヲ他人ヨリ受ル人ヨリ賤キハナシ、凡ソ人ノ斯世ニ生レ有用ノ人ト稱セラルヽハ、地位ニ在ラズシテ、言行儀範ニ在リ、故ニ吾身ノ遭際、極テ卑陋ナリ𪜈、一世ノ風化ニ關係スル有用ノ人トナルヿヲ得ベシ、譬バ光明赫奕タル物ヲ、低處ニ置が如シ、ソノ四方ヲ照ヿ、山上ニ置モノト異ナルヿナシ、眞正ノ人ハ、ソノ出トコロノ地位ヲ擇バズ、或ハ沼澤ノ茅舍ニ長ジ、或ハ城市ノ陋巷ニ養レ、或ハ農民ノ中ニ混ジ、或ハ工人ノ中ニ雜ル、サレバ、僅ニ墳墓ノ用ニ充ベキホドノ小々ノ土地ヲ耕セル貧民ト雖𪜈、千萬人ノ產業ヲ受繼ベキホドニ、信實ノ行ヲ崇シ、善良ノ志ヲ立ルヲ得ベシ、凡常ノ工舖ト雖𪜈、ソノ人ノ志行ニ由テ、コレヲシテ、或ハ工事勉强ノ學校トナスベク、學術ノ學校トナスベク、德行ノ學校トナスベシ、或ハ懶惰ノ學校トナスベク、癡愚ノ學校トナスベク、邪惡ノ學校トナスベシ、蓋シ邦國敎化ノ行ルヽヿハ、人民各箇ノ志行ニ關係シ、及ビ各ソノ地位ニ隨テ、機會ヲ失ズ、善事ヲ行ニ賴ルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: Thus, every act we do or word we utter, as well as every act we witness or word we hear, carries with it an influence which extends over, and gives a colour, not only to the whole of our future life, but makes itself felt upon the whole frame of society. We may not, and indeed cannot, possibly, trace the influence working itself into action in its various ramifications amongst our children, our friends, or associates; yet there it is assuredly, working on for ever. And herein lies the great significance of setting forth a good example,—a silent teaching which even the poorest and least significant person can practise in his daily life. There is no one so humble, but that he owes to others this simple but priceless instruction. Even the meanest condition may thus be made useful; for the light set in a low place shines as faithfully as that set upon a hill. Everywhere, and under almost all circumstances, however externally adverse—in moorland shielings, in cottage hamlets, in the close alleys of great towns—the true man may grow. He who tills a space of earth scarce bigger than is needed for his grave, may work as faithfully, and to as good purpose, as the heir to thousands. The commonest workshop may thus be a school of industry, science, and good morals, on the one hand; or of idleness, folly, and depravity, on the other. It all depends on the individual men, and the use they make of the opportunities for good which offer themselves.

chu.a: 抑モ世ニ二種ノ人アリ
chu.n: 原文は「どれほど身分の低い人でも、この簡素な、しかし値のつけられない教えを、他人に対して負うている」の一文。人を教化する人とされる人の二種がある、という所は中村が言い換えて加えたもの

chu.a: 千萬人ノ產業ヲ受繼ベキホドニ

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 善過タル一生、正直ナル品行ハ、子孫及ビ天下ニ、遺予ル大產業ナリ、蓋シコレ德行ヲ勸ル爲ノ極妙ノ辯說トナリ、惡行ヲ箴ル爲ノ極嚴ノ呵責トナルベシ、金銀田產ノ遺予ルモノハ、散失スルヿアルベケレ𪜈、コノ產資ハ原泉ノ竭ザルが如ク、永ク相繼續スベキナリ、勞爾德花未、甞テ波伯ヲ謗毀セシ時、波伯コレニ答テ、吾父母ノ如モノハ我ヲシテ、一ノ愧色ヲ顯シメズ、彼が如キ子ハ、ソノ父母一粒ノ涕淚ニモ値ラズト云リシトナリ、
blocks.genbun: A life well spent, a character uprightly sustained, is no slight legacy to leave to one’s children, and to the world; for it is the most eloquent lesson of virtue and the severest reproof of vice, while it continues an enduring source of the best kind of riches. Well for those who can say, as Pope did, in rejoinder to the sarcasm of Lord Hervey, “I think it enough that my parents, such as they were, never cost me a blush, and that their son, such as he is, never cost them a tear.”

chu.n: 原文の「その息子」はポープ自身のこと。「私の両親は私に一度も顔を赤らめさせず、その息子（私）は両親に一度も涙を流させなかった」と言う。相手のハーヴィー卿を指すとした中村の訳は原文と違う。金銀田産は散り失せるが、という対比は中村が加えたもの

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 八　實行ノ人ヲ化スルヿ、空言ノ比スベキニ非ズ
blocks.text: 空言ヲ以テ敎ルハ、實行ヲ以テ敎ルニ若ズ、是故ニ眞實ノ心アル人ハ、卑賤ノ地位ニ居ルト雖𪜈、心力ヲ奮ヒ、實事ヲ行フナリ、他人ニ對シテ、一句敎訓ノ語ヲ道ザレ𪜈、自ラ世人ヲシテ、眼ノアタリ、ソノ行實ヲ觀ルヨリ、感發激勵シテ、コレニ倣ハント欲スルノ志ヲ生ゼシメ、後起ノ人ヲ、造リ出セリ、托馬士。來的ノ罪人ヲ惠恤スルヿヲ以テ、口頭ノ話說トナセシヲ聞ズ、潤。邦治ノ襤褸ナル子女ヲ敎訓スルヿヲ以テ、口頭ノ話說トナセシヲ聞ズ、二人、タヾ一意ニソノ目的ヲ行ルノミ、然𪜈、コノ極卑極貧ナル二人ノ默然トシテ行フトコロノモノ、ソノ能一世ヲ風靡スルヿ、タヾ千言萬語ノ敎訓ノミニアラズ、タヾ大聲壯語ノ號令ノミニ非ズ、來的ノ事ハ、既ニ第十編ニ見ユ、革斯里、邦治ノ儀型ヲ觀テ、大ニコレニ感ジ、遂ニソノ繼述者トナリシヿヲ、自ラ記錄セル文アリ、次ニ引ベシ、邦治ハ、波都毛士ノ補鞋工ニシテ、革斯里ハ、貧家子女ノ爲ニ義學ヲ興セシ首唱ノ人ナリ、
blocks.genbun:
It is not enough to tell others what they are to do, but to exhibit the actual example of doing. What Mrs. Chisholm described to Mrs. Stowe as the secret of her success, applies to all life. “I found,” she said, “that if we want anything done, we must go to work and do: it is of no use merely to talk—none whatever.” It is poor eloquence that only shows how a person can talk. Had Mrs. Chisholm rested satisfied with lecturing, her project, she was persuaded, would never have got beyond the region of talk; but when people saw what she was doing and had actually accomplished, they fell in with her views and came forward to help her. Hence the most beneficent worker is not he who says the most eloquent things, or even who thinks the most loftily, but he who does the most eloquent acts.
True-hearted persons, even in the humblest station in life, who are energetic doers, may thus give an impulse to good works out of all proportion, apparently, to their actual station in society. Thomas Wright might have talked about the reclamation of criminals, and John Pounds about the necessity for Ragged Schools, and yet done nothing; instead of which they simply set to work without any other idea in their minds than that of doing, not talking. And how the example of even the poorest man may tell upon society, hear what Dr. Guthrie, the apostle of the Ragged School movement, says of the influence which the example of John Pounds, the humble Portsmouth cobbler, exercised upon his own working career:—

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 九　邦治鞋ヲ補ナガラニ修金ナキ貧兒ヲ敎シ事
blocks.text: 革斯里曰、吾義學ヲ世ニ興サント志シ、コノ事ヲ以テ吾任トナセシハ、極テ些微ノ事ヨリ激發セラレタリ、人ノ身世ハ、川流ノ水ノ如ク、始ヨリソノ趣トコロヲ期セザレ𪜈、自ラソノ往トコロノ路ヲ覓メ得ルヿ、蓋シ天命ノ然ラシムルトコロナリ、予多年前ニ、上帝道學士查爾馬斯ノ桑梓ナルフヲアスノ海口ニ遊シ時、一ノ旅館ニ入リ、飮食ヲ取シニ、ソノ房中ヲ見ルニ、女伴羊ヲ牧スル圖アリ、コレハ吾心ニ中ホドニモ非ズ、然ニソノ火爐眉ノ上ヲ見レバ、大ナル印刷ノ畫アリテ、補鞋工房中ノ景ヲ描ガケルモノアリ、コノ補鞋工、鼻上ニ眼鏡ヲ掛ケ、一ノ舊鞋ヲ、ソノ膝間ニ置リ、額廣ク、口堅ク、髙大ノ志氣アル人ト疑ハル、數多ノ童子女兒、襤褸ノ衣裝ヲ着ルモノ、コレヲ圍繞シテ、ソノ課業ヲ學ブ、補鞋工ソノ忙ハシキ手工ヲ做ツヽ、コノ貧キ子女ヲ敎ヘ、仁愛ノ光一室ヲ照耀セリ、予コノ圖ヲ觀テ、奇ナルヿニ思ヒ、詳カニコレヲ知ントテ、ソノ題言ヲ讀バ、コノ人ハ、潤。邦治トイヘル波都毛士ノ補鞋工ナリ、貧家ノ子女、街衢ニ嬉遊シ、敎育ヲ受ズシテ、惡習ヲ長ジ、廢物トナレ𪜈、敎士コレヲ憐ズ、官吏コレヲ察セズ、鄕紳コレヲ救ハザルヲ、邦治獨リ惻然トシテ、之ヲ悲ミ、良牧人ノ如ク、コノ襤褸ナル子女ヲ聚メテ、コレヲ上帝ノ道ニ導ビキ、人世ノ學業ヲ敎ヘ、每日工事ヲ勉メ、額ヨリ出セル汗ヲ以テ、僅ニ口糧ヲ得、過活ヲ做ル間ニ、修金ナキ子女ヲ敎育シ、既ニ五百人餘ヲ救ヒ出セリト、記シテゾアリケル、予コレヲ讀畢リテ後、赧然トシテ自ラ耻ヂ、從前ノ行事ヲ默省スルニ、他人ノ爲、一世ノ爲トナレルヿ、幾何モアラズ、然ルニコノ人、極卑極賤ノ境界ニ在ナガラ、カヽル仁善ノ大功勞ヲ、美シクモ成ルモノカナト、吾心ニ且ハ耻ヂ且ハ感ジ、意ズモ聲ヲ出シテ、同伴セル友ニ向ヒ、コノ人ヲコソ眞正ノ仁者ト名ヅクベケレ、不列顚海岸ノ中ニ、未曾有ノ大ナル紀功碑ヲ、コノ人ノ爲メニコソ建ベケレト言ケリ、抑モ、造化ノ大主、貧シキ子女ノ敎育ヲ受ザルヲ悲ミ玉ヒ、コノ人ノ心ヲ默啓シ、一世ノ倡首ト爲シメ玉フニ疑ナシ、潤。邦治ハ、獨リ仁人ノミナラズ、亦智者ナリ、ソノ貧兒ヲ招キ敎フルニ、ポリスメン〔巡吏〕ノ如ニ、勢ヲ以テコレヲ驅迫スルニ非ズ、熱キ蕃薯ヲ弊衣ノ間ニ携ヘ、己が如キ弊衣ナル子女ノ鼻下ニ蕃薯ヲ近ヅク、カクシテ、コレヲ家ニ延敎ヘタリシトナリ、

ruby.r: テガラナシルシスキヒ

blocks.genbun: “The interest I have been led to take in this cause is an example of how, in Providence, a man’s destiny—his course of life, like that of a river—may be determined and affected by very trivial circumstances. It is rather curious—at least it is interesting to me to remember—that it was by a picture I was first led to take an interest in ragged schools—by a picture in an old, obscure, decaying burgh that stands on the shores of the Frith of Forth, the birthplace of Thomas Chalmers. I went to see this place many years ago; and, going into an inn for refreshment, I found the room covered with pictures of shepherdesses with their crooks, and sailors in holiday attire, not particularly interesting. But above the chimney-piece there was a large print, more respectable than its neighbours, which represented a cobbler’s room. The cobbler was there himself, spectacles on nose, an old shoe between his knees—the massive forehead and firm mouth indicating great determination of character, and, beneath his bushy eyebrows, benevolence gleamed out on a number of poor ragged boys and girls who stood at their lessons round the busy cobbler. My curiosity was awakened; and in the inscription I read how this man, John Pounds, a cobbler in Portsmouth, taking pity on the multitude of poor ragged children left by ministers and magistrates, and ladies and gentlemen, to go to ruin on the streets—how, like a good shepherd, he gathered in these wretched outcasts—how he had trained them to God and to the world—and how, while earning his daily bread by the sweat of his brow, he had rescued from misery and saved to society not less than five hundred of these children. I felt ashamed of myself. I felt reproved for the little I had done. My feelings were touched. I was astonished at this man’s achievements; and I well remember, in the enthusiasm of the moment, saying to my companion (and I have seen in my cooler and calmer moments no reason for unsaying the saying)—‘That man is an honour to humanity, and deserves the tallest monument ever raised within the shores of Britain.’ I took up that man’s history, and I found it animated by the spirit of Him who ‘had compassion on the multitude.’ John Pounds was a clever man besides; and, like Paul, if he could not win a poor boy any other way, he won him by art. He would be seen chasing a ragged boy along the quays, and compelling him to come to school, not by the power of a policeman, but by the power of a hot potato. He knew the love an Irishman had for a potato; and John Pounds might be seen running holding under the boy’s nose a potato, like an Irishman, very hot, and with a coat as ragged as himself.

chu.a: 女伴羊ヲ牧スル圖アリ
chu.n: 原文は、杖を持った羊飼いの娘たちと、晴れ着の水夫たちの絵が部屋じゅうに掛かっていた、と言う。水夫の絵は中村の訳にはない。靴直しの「濃い眉」も省かれている
原文はここに、かっこに入れて「のちに冷静に落ち着いて考えても、この言葉を取り消す理由は見当たらない」と添える。中村の訳にはない

chu.a: 造化ノ大主、貧シキ子女ノ敎育ヲ受ザルヲ悲ミ玉ヒ
chu.n: 原文は「私はこの人の伝記を手に取り、それが『群衆を憐れんだ』方の精神に生かされているのを知った」。神がこの人の心を啓いて一世の先がけとした、という中村の訳は言い換え。続く「パウロのように、ほかの手で得られなければ、策をもって得た」も省かれている

chu.a: 熱キ蕃薯ヲ弊衣ノ間ニ携ヘ
chu.n: 原文では、ぼろをまとっているのはじゃがいも（皮の破れた熱いじゃがいも）で、少年のぼろ着になぞらえた冗談。波止場でぼろ着の少年を追いかけたこと、アイルランド人がじゃがいもを好むことを知っていたという所は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 予思フニ、末日審判ノ期至リ、善人尊榮ヲ受ベキノ時、コノ塵世ニ於テ、詩人ニ功德ヲ贊セラレ、大石ニ勞績ヲ勒セラルヽノ人、及ビ生時權勢爵位アルノ人、雲霞ノ如ニ來リ聚レル中ニ於テ、造化ノ大主、特ニコノ側陋貧塞ナル老人ヲ、ソノ前ニ召ビ近ケラレ、コレニ宣テ、汝善事ヲ吾兒子ニ施セリ、即チ我ニ施セシニ同ジトテ、厚クコレヲ賞シ玉フベキナリ、
blocks.genbun: When the day comes when honour will be done to whom honour is due, I can fancy the crowd of those whose fame poets have sung, and to whose memory monuments have been raised, dividing like the wave, and, passing the great, and the noble, and the mighty of the land, this poor, obscure old man stepping forward and receiving the especial notice of Him who said ‘Inasmuch as ye did it to one of the least of these, ye did it also to Me.’”

chu.a: 汝善事ヲ吾兒子ニ施セリ
chu.n: 新約聖書マタイによる福音書 25 章 40 節の言葉。原文は「これらの最も小さい者の一人にしたのは、すなわち私にしたのである」

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十　朋友ノ擇ベキ事
blocks.text: 凡ソ人ハ、常ニ知ズ覺ズ、己ニ伴フモノヽ品行風習、及ソノ議論ニ甄陶鎔鑄セラルルモノナリ、蓋シ規則ノ善モノ、固ヨリ人ヲ資益スベケレ𪜈、コレヲ要スルニ、好模範ノ人ヲ資益スルニ如ズ、好キ模範ハ、他人ヲシテ實行ニ與ラシムルノ眞益アリ、縱ヒ口ニ良善ノ訓戒ヲ言𪜈、身ニ壞惡ノ表樣ヲ立ナバ、譬バ右手ヲ以テ家ヲ建テ、左手ヲ以テ之ヲ曳倒が如シ、何ノ益アランヤ、サレバ、人ノ朋友ヲ擇ビ、交遊ヲ愼ハ、甚ダ緊要ナル事ナリ、
blocks.genbun: The education of character is very much a question of models; we mould ourselves so unconsciously after the characters, manners, habits, and opinions of those who are about us. Good rules may do much, but good models far more; for in the latter we have instruction in action—wisdom at work. Good admonition and bad example only build with one hand to pull down with the other. Hence the vast importance of exercising great care in the selection of companions,

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 就中少年ノ人、コヽニ著眼セザルベカラズ、蓋シ少年ノ人、相朋トシ好ズルハ、磁石ノ親和吸引スルが如ク、自ラ互ヒニ相ヒ似スルヿナリ、義地活士オモヘラク、人ハ、常々徃來スル朋友ト、感情相通ジ、聲氣相應ジ、自ラ相視倣モノナレバ、絕好ノ模範ヲ擇ヲ以テ、最要ノ事ト爲ベシ、義氏ノ記號トスル語ニ「ノー、コムパニー、ヲル、グード、コムパニー、」朋友ナシ、有レバ必ズ好朋友、ト云リ、勞爾德格林烏德、甞テ一少年ニ書ヲ寄テ曰、卑陋ナル人ヲ以テ朋友ト爲ンヨリハ、寧ロ間居獨處ヲ以テ愈レリト爲ス、コノ語ヲ訓戒トシテ、常ニ守ルベシ、人ノ品價ハ、常ニソノ朋友ノ品價優等ナルモノニ管治セラルヽモノナリ、故ニ汝ノ朋友ハ、必ズ汝ノ如ク、或ハ汝ニ勝モノナラシムベシ、醫師悉田寒ノ論ニ曰、人誰ニ限ズ、時トシテハ前ヨリ善、時トシテハ前ヨリ惡クナルモノナリ、コレ他ノ故ニ非ズ、或ハ善人ニ接シ、或ハ不善ノ人ト相ヒ談ズルニ由レリト云リ、畫家比達。立里ハ、決シテ惡畫ヲ目ニ觸ズト、規則ヲ立タリ、コレ惡畫ノ、ソノ筆ニ傳染スルヲ恐ルが故ナリ、人ノ言行、マタ然リ、常ニ汚辱ナル人ノ樣式ヲ見慣レ、下流ナル人ノ集會ニ伍スルモノハ、自ラソレト化シテ、同氣一體トナルヿヲ免ザルベキナリ、
blocks.genbun: especially in youth. There is a magnetic affinity in young persons which insensibly tends to assimilate them to each other’s likeness. Mr. Edgeworth was so strongly convinced that from sympathy they involuntarily imitated or caught the tone of the company they frequented, that he held it to be of the most essential importance that they should be taught to select the very best models. “No company, or good company,” was his motto. Lord Collingwood, writing to a young friend, said, “Hold it as a maxim that you had better be alone than in mean company. Let your companions be such as yourself, or superior; for the worth of a man will always be ruled by that of his company.” It was a remark of the famous Dr. Sydenham that everybody some time or other would be the better or the worse for having but spoken to a good or a bad man. As Sir Peter Lely made it a rule never to look at a bad picture if he could help it, believing that whenever he did so his pencil caught a taint from it, so, whoever chooses to gaze often upon a debased specimen of humanity and to frequent his society, cannot help gradually assimilating himself to that sort of model.

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十一　觀感ノ益
blocks.text: 是故ニ、少年ノ人ハ、良朋善友ノ自己ヨリ高等ナルモノヲ求メテ模範トナシ、コレト齊シカランヿヲ望ベシ、國政學ノ名家弗蘭西士。花納爾曰、吾進脩ノ益ヲ得タルハ、志高學邃キ諸名士ト博ク交リシニ由ヿ、書册上ヨリ得タルモノヨリ多シト、勞爾德舍爾畔、少年ノ時、馬爾士海伯〔法國有名ノ公師〕ヲ一タビ訪シ時、深クコレニ感服セリ、後コノ事ヲ言テ「予處々ニ行旅シ、許多ノ人士ニ逢シガ、馬爾士海伯ニ感化セラレシガ如ヿアラズ、今ヨリ後一生ノ間、何等ノ善事ヲ做行フ𪜈、馬氏ノ聲容ヲ憶起スルニヨリテ、吾精神ヲ激發スルニ疑ナシト云リ、勃古斯敦少時駕乃家ノ儀範ヲ觀シ時、自修ルノ志氣ヲ發シ、生平ノ品行ヲ造リ出セリト言シトナリ、善人君子ニ接見スレバ、必ズ我ニ善德ヲ分チ與フルヿ、萬ニ一ヲモ失ズ、恰モ花草ノ芬芳ナルモノ、行人ノ衣裳ヲ薰シ、久ウシテ散ゼザルが如シ、潤。斯打林ハ、德卲ク識高キ人ナリ、コレト相遇モノヲシテ、ソノ心志ヲ警發シ、當做ノ事ヲ知ラシメ、ソノ人品ヲシテ高カラシメタリ、故ニ斯氏ノ丰采ニ接スルニ賴テ、自脩ノ道ニ進シヿヲ招認スル人、世ニ多カリキ、篤連知、斯氏ヲ評シテ曰、彼人ニ遇ヒ、ソノ貴キ性格ト、相觸ルトキハ、忽チ自カラ吾が身ノ貴クナリテ、高處ニ提起セラルヽヲ覺ユ、退イテ吾が未ダコレニ接セザルノ前ヲ顧ミレバ、ソノ心志ノ住スルトコロ、尋常庸俗ノ田地ナリシヿヲ見得タリ、蓋シ彼人ト相晤スル每ニ、見識ノ高明ニ進ムヲ覺エザルヿナカリキト云リ、コレ等ニ由テ觀ルトキハ、品行ノ尊貴ナルモノハ、ソノ運動作用、時トシテ輟ヿナク常ニ他人ノコレニ附近シ接見スル人ヲシテ、自ラコレト共ニ尊貴ナラシメ、コレト共ニ化シテ自ラ知ザラシム、嗚呼人心ノ感應、善行ノ神通力、カクノ如シ、至奇至妙トコソ云フベケレ、
notes: 馬氏享保六年生寬政六年被殺
斯氏文化三年生弘化元年歿以文章名タイムス新聞紙作者也
blocks.genbun:
It is therefore advisable for young men to seek the fellowship of the good, and always to aim at a higher standard than themselves. Francis Horner, speaking of the advantages to himself of direct personal intercourse with high-minded, intelligent men, said, “I cannot hesitate to decide that I have derived more intellectual improvement from them than from all the books I have turned over.” Lord Shelburne (afterwards Marquis of Lansdowne), when a young man, paid a visit to the venerable Malesherbes, and was so much impressed by it, that he said,—“I have travelled much, but I have never been so influenced by personal contact with any man; and if I ever accomplish any good in the course of my life, I am certain that the recollection of M. de Malesherbes will animate my soul.” So Fowell Buxton was always ready to acknowledge the powerful influence exercised upon the formation of his character in early life by the example of the Gurney family: “It has given a colour to my life,” he used to say. Speaking of his success at the Dublin University, he confessed, “I can ascribe it to nothing but my Earlham visits.” It was from the Gurneys he “caught the infection” of self-improvement.
Contact with the good never fails to impart good, and we carry away with us some of the blessing, as travellers’ garments retain the odour of the flowers and shrubs through which they have passed. Those who knew the late John Sterling intimately, have spoken of the beneficial influence which he exercised on all with whom he came into personal contact. Many owed to him their first awakening to a higher being; from him they learnt what they were, and what they ought to be. Mr. Trench says of him:—“It was impossible to come in contact with his noble nature without feeling one’s self in some measure ennobled and lifted up, as I ever felt when I left him, into a higher region of objects and aims than that in which one is tempted habitually to dwell.” It is thus that the noble character always acts; we become insensibly elevated by him, and cannot help feeling as he does and acquiring the habit of looking at things in the same light. Such is the magical action and reaction of minds upon each other.

chu.a: 馬爾士海伯〔法國有名ノ公師〕
chu.n: かっこの中の説明は中村が加えたもの。原文は「高齢のマルゼルブ」。シェルバーン卿に添えた「のちのランズダウン侯」は、中村の訳にはない

chu.a: 勃古斯敦少時駕乃家ノ儀範ヲ觀シ時
chu.n: 原文にあるバクストンの二つの言葉（「それは私の生涯に色を与えた」、ダブリン大学での成功は「アーラム訪問のほかには帰するものがない」）は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十二　畫家、樂工、己ニ優ルモノヲ慕フ事
blocks.text: 工藝ノ人、マタ己ヨリ優レル人ト、相交ハルニ由テ、ソノ技ノ進タルヿヲ、多ク招認セリ、サレバ、樂工海同ノ巧技ハ、罕垤爾ニ由テ、激發セラレタリ、海同甞テ罕垤爾ノ樂ヲ奏スルヲ聽テ、甚ダコレヲ熱愛シ、コレヨリ、樂曲ヲ作ント思起セリ、自言ヒケルハ、予モシコノ事ナカリセバ、クリエーシヨンハ、吾手ヨリ出ザルベシト、クリエーシヨンハ、ソノ作ル有名ノ樂曲ナリ、又曰ク、罕氏ノ樂ヲ聽トキハ、電ニ擊ルヽが如キヲ覺ユト、マタ罕氏ノ曲、未ダ予血ヲ引出サヾルモノアラズト云リ、畫家挪斯可的、少カリシ時、禮諾爾圖ノ畫ヲ好ミ、コレヲ慕ヿ甚シ、一日禮氏、的分舍ニ來リ、集會ノ席ニ在シ時、挪斯可的、群聚ノ中ヲ推シ入リ、禮氏ノ外衣ノ裾ニ觸ルヽホドニ切近セリ、挪斯可的、後ソノ事ヲ言テ曰、予カク近ヅキ、ソノ衣裾ニ觸シ時、吾心ヲ快足慰滿セシヿ、眞ニイハンカタナカリキト、嗚呼コレゾ少年ノ熱心好慕ヨリ出ル眞正ノ感觸トハ云ベキ、
blocks.genbun: Artists, also, feel themselves elevated by contact with artists greater than themselves. Thus Haydn’s genius was first fired by Handel. Hearing him play, Haydn’s ardour for musical composition was at once excited, and but for this circumstance, he himself believed that he would never have written the ‘Creation.’ Speaking of Handel, he said, “When he chooses, he strikes like the thunderbolt;” and at another time, “There is not a note of him but draws blood.” Scarlatti was another of Handel’s ardent admirers, following him all over Italy; afterwards, when speaking of the great master, he would cross himself in token of admiration. True artists never fail generously to recognise each other’s greatness. Thus Beethoven’s admiration for Cherubini was regal: and he ardently hailed the genius of Schubert: “Truly,” said he, “in Schubert dwells a divine fire.” When Northcote was a mere youth he had such an admiration for Reynolds that, when the great painter was once attending a public meeting down in Devonshire, the boy pushed through the crowd, and got so near Reynolds as to touch the skirt of his coat, “which I did,” says Northcote, “with great satisfaction to my mind,”—a true touch of youthful enthusiasm in its admiration of genius.

chu.a: クリエーシヨンハ、ソノ作ル有名ノ樂曲ナリ
chu.n: この説明は中村が加えたもの。『天地創造』はハイドンのオラトリオ
原文は「彼は、その気になれば、雷のように打つ」と、ヘンデルの音楽の力を言う
原文はこの前に、ヘンデルをイタリアじゅう追って歩いたスカルラッティ、ケルビーニとシューベルトをたたえたベートーヴェンの話を置く。中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十三　勇將ノ表樣
blocks.text: 勇將勁卒ノ表樣、大ニ怯夫ヲシテ氣勢ヲ激發セシムルヿナリ、サレバ、尋常ノ人ニヲモ、勇將ニ率ラルヽ時ハ、毛髮皮肉、コレガ爲メニ飛動シ、化シテ勇士トナリテ、自ラ覺ヘズ、且コレノミナラズ、勇將酣戰ノ狀、人ヲシテコレヲ回憶スルコトニ、血氣奮興シ、喇叭ノ聲ヲ聞が如ヲ覺エシム、的士加ハ、薄希米亞ノ勇將ナリ、死スル時、遺言シテ、ソノ身ノ皮ヲ以テ、戰皷ニ張シム、コレソノ軍衆ノ勇氣ヲ激發センガ爲ナリ、以比臘斯ノ王斯干垤爾味具、死セシ時、突厥ノ人、ソノ骨ヲ乞得テ、各一小屑ヲ心胸ニ貼附シ、カクシテ、ソノ剛勇ヲ分チ得ント思ヒシカバ、果シテ戰場ニ於テ、屢ゝ靈驗アルヲ覺エシトナリ、蘇葛蘭ノ猛將道額拉斯ハ、ソノ王普魯斯ノ命ニ從ヒ、王沒シテ後、ソノ心肝ヲ匣ニシ、コレヲ首ニ掛テ、パレスタインニ徃キ、合戰セシ時、ソノ驍騎ノ兵、敵兵ニ圍レ、危ク見エシカバ、道額拉斯、王ノ心肝ヲ藏スル銀匣ヲ以テ、稠密ナル敵兵ノ中ニ投ジテ、大音ヲ揚テ、進ヤ兵ドモ、勵ミ戰ヒ、汝ノ勇ヲ顯セヨ、道額拉斯汝等ニ續キテ討死スベシト言ツヽ、敵衆ノ中ニ衝入シトゾ、
blocks.genbun: The example of the brave is an inspiration to the timid, their presence thrilling through every fibre. Hence the miracles of valour so often performed by ordinary men under the leadership of the heroic. The very recollection of the deeds of the valiant stirs men’s blood like the sound of a trumpet. Ziska bequeathed his skin to be used as a drum to inspire the valour of the Bohemians. When Scanderbeg, prince of Epirus, was dead, the Turks wished to possess his bones, that each might wear a piece next his heart, hoping thus to secure some portion of the courage he had displayed while living, and which they had so often experienced in battle. When the gallant Douglas, bearing the heart of Bruce to the Holy Land, saw one of his knights surrounded and sorely pressed by the Saracens, he took from his neck the silver case containing the hero’s bequest, and throwing it amidst the thickest press of his foes, cried, “Pass first in fight, as thou wert wont to do, and Douglas will follow thee, or die;” and so saying, he rushed forward to the place where it fell, and was there slain.

chu.n: 原文は「彼が生前に示し、トルコ人が戦場でたびたび身をもって味わった勇気」。骨を身につけて戦場で効き目があった、という中村の訳は原文と違う

chu.a: ソノ王普魯斯ノ命ニ從ヒ
chu.n: 王の遺命によるという説明は中村が加えたもの。原文は「ブルースの心臓を聖地へ運んでいた勇敢なダグラス」。相手はサラセン人とある
原文では、ダグラスは投げた王の心臓に向かって「いつものように、戦いの先頭を行かれよ。ダグラスはあなたに従うか、さもなくば死ぬ」と叫ぶ。兵に呼びかけたとする中村の訳は原文と違う。ダグラスがそこで討たれたという結びも、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十四　言行錄ヲ讀ヨリシテ感發奮興セシ人ノ例ヲ擧グ
blocks.text: 眞正ノ人ト稱セラルベキ人ノ言行ヲ記載スル書ハ、中ニ貴重ナル種子ヲ包藏ス、蓋シソノ人、骨已ニ朽ト雖𪜈、ソノ聲音ナホ生ルガ如ク、ソノ智識、ナホソノ中ニ儼存セリ、彌爾敦曰ク、言行錄ハ、大人君子ノ生ル血ナリ、香料ヲ以テ腐壞ヲ防キ、謹ミ貯テ、後世ニ遺セルモノナリ、ト云リ、蓋シ極高ノ言行、極善ノ儀範ハ、人心ヲ鎔鑄スルヿ、百代ノ遠ニ及ビ、後人ヲシテ企慕追求セシムルナリ、コヽニ後人ヲ葡萄ニ喩ヘ、先哲ヲ日ニ喩ヘタル詩アリ、證ト爲ベシ、
blocks.genbun: The chief use of biography consists in the noble models of character in which it abounds. Our great forefathers still live among us in the records of their lives, as well as in the acts they have done, which live also; still sit by us at table, and hold us by the hand; furnishing examples for our benefit, which we may still study, admire and imitate. Indeed, whoever has left behind him the record of a noble life, has bequeathed to posterity an enduring source of good, for it serves as a model for others to form themselves by in all time to come; still breathing fresh life into men, helping them to reproduce his life anew, and to illustrate his character in other forms. Hence a book containing the life of a true man is full of precious seed. It is a still living voice; it is an intellect. To use Milton’s words, “it is the precious life-blood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up on purpose to a life beyond life.” Such a book never ceases to exercise an elevating and ennobling influence. But, above all, there is the Book containing the very highest Example set before us to shape our lives by in this world—the most suitable for all the necessities of our mind and heart—an example which we can only follow afar off and feel after,

chu.a: 眞正ノ人ト稱セラルベキ人ノ言行ヲ記載スル書ハ
chu.n: 原文の段落の初めの三文（伝記の主な効用は気高い人格の手本にある、偉大な祖先は今も食卓でわれわれのそばに座り手を取っている、気高い生涯の記録を残した人は後の世に尽きない善の源を遺した）は、中村の訳にはない

chu.a: 蓋シ極高ノ言行、極善ノ儀範ハ
chu.n: 原文はここで、最高の手本を収めた「あの書」、すなわち聖書のことを言い、その手本は遠くから従い、手探りで求めるほかない、として次の詩につなぐ。中村は聖書に触れず、先哲の言行一般のこととして訳し、詩の喩えの説明を加えている

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 葡萄ノ天日ヲ見タルヿナキモノアリ、然𪜈天日ヲ夢ニ見、天日ノ在ル所ヲ憶度シ、務メテ高處ニ攀上テ、遂ニ天日ノ光ヲ受タリ、
blocks.genbun: “Like plants or vines which never saw the sun, But dream of him and guess where he may be, And do their best to climb and get to him.”

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 少年ノ人、荀モ勃古斯敦、亞瑙爾德ノ如キ人ノ言行錄ヲ讀タランニハ、必ズ自ラ良善ノ心、書ヨリ加リ、堅剛ノ志、書ヨリ倍スルヲ覺ベシ、カクノ如キ書ハ、人ヲシテ人タル所以ノ道ヲ知リ、人ノ爲シ得ベキノ事ヲ曉リ、希望ノ心ヲシテ益ゝ堅カラシメ、終身ノ志行ヲシテ、高明ノ域ニ進マシムベシ、マタ技藝ニ妙絕ナル人ノ傳記ハ、技藝ニ志ス人ヲ、勸勉激勵スルヿ、甚ダ大イナリ、意太利有名ノ畫家格列日窩、少キ時、彌開爾。安日洛ノ傳ヲ讀ミ、ソノ作ルモノヲ想像シ、意ズ聲ヲ放テ、我マタ一箇ノ畫工ナリト云テ、コレヨリ畫ヲ始テ學シトナリ、撒母耳羅彌爾禮ハ、法國ノ尙書達凱肖ノ傳ヲヨミテ、感憤ノ志ヲ生セシヿヲ、自ラ作ル傳ニ言リ、曰、予昔トマスノ著書ヲ披閱シ、偶ゝ達凱肖ノ賛ヲ讀ミ、ソノ高志卓行ノ尊敬スベキモノヲ觀テ、大ニ吾熱愛追慕ノ心ヲ起シ、コレヨリ塵世ノ榮貴ヲ卑視シテ、眞榮眞實ノ路ニ進ムベキ門徑ヲ求得タリト云リ、

ruby.r: サミュールロミルレイ

blocks.genbun: Again, no young man can rise from the perusal of such lives as those of Buxton and Arnold, without feeling his mind and heart made better, and his best resolves invigorated. Such biographies increase a man’s self-reliance by demonstrating what men can be, and what they can do; fortifying his hopes and elevating his aims in life. Sometimes a young man discovers himself in a biography, as Correggio felt within him the risings of genius on contemplating the works of Michael Angelo: “And I too, am a painter,” he exclaimed. Sir Samuel Romilly, in his autobiography, confessed himself to have been powerfully influenced by the life of the great and noble-minded French Chancellor Daguesseau:—“The works of Thomas,” says he, “had fallen into my hands, and I had read with admiration his ‘Eloge of Daguesseau;’ and the career of honour which he represented that illustrious magistrate to have run, excited to a great degree my ardour and ambition, and opened to my imagination new paths of glory.”

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十五　富蘭克林、德留、達德禮
blocks.text: 富蘭克林、少年ノ時、亞米利加有名ナル上帝道學士格董。馬沙ノエスセース、トー、ドー、グード〔作善文〕即チ自ラソノ生平ノ事ヲ錄セル書ヲ讀シヿ、後來卓犖ノ傑タル基礎トハナレリ、撒母耳。德留ハ、ソノ一生、職事ニ勉强スルヿ、慣テ性トナリタルハ、富蘭克林ノ著述ニ遺セル儀範ヲ師トシ學シニ由リト云リ、カク馬沙ヨリ富蘭克林ニ傳リ、富氏ヨリ德留ニ傳ルガ如ク、好儀範ノ將來ニ傳ルヿ、何ゾ底極スルトコロアランヤ、コノ故ニ書ヲ讀ムハ、友ヲ取ルガ如シ、ソノ極善ナルモノヲ擇ンデ、コレト親熟シ、ソノ中ニ含タル嘉言偉績ヲ師法トシ、コレニ跂及センヿヲ期スベキナリ、勞爾德達德禮曰、吾が好ンデ讀トコロノ書ハ、昔ヨリ習熟シタルモノナリ、予レ極善ノ書ヲ擇ビ朋友ト做シ、益ゝコレト親熟センコトヲ求メ、浪ニソノ他ニ及バズ、蓋予舊書ヲ温スルハ、新書ヲ讀ニ比スレバ、九倍ノ益アルヲ覺ユト云リ、
blocks.genbun: Franklin was accustomed to attribute his usefulness and eminence to his having early read Cotton Mather’s ‘Essays to do Good’—a book which grew out of Mather’s own life. And see how good example draws other men after it, and propagates itself through future generations in all lands. For Samuel Drew avers that he framed his own life, and especially his business habits, after the model left on record by Benjamin Franklin. Thus it is impossible to say where a good example may not reach, or where it will end, if indeed it have an end. Hence the advantage, in literature as in life, of keeping the best society, reading the best books, and wisely admiring and imitating the best things we find in them. “In literature,” said Lord Dudley, “I am fond of confining myself to the best company, which consists chiefly of my old acquaintance, with whom I am desirous of becoming more intimate; and I suspect that nine times out of ten it is more profitable, if not more agreeable, to read an old book over again, than to read a new one for the first time.”

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十六　亞爾費立、雷閥拉、路楊、烏爾弗、加禮
blocks.text: 人或ハ始メ消閒ノ具トナスノミノ目的ヲ以テ、偶古人ノ言行錄ヲ讀ミ、コレヨリ平生ニアラザル大勢力ヲ生ジ、進脩ノ志ヲ勵シ、遂ニ卓節偉行ノ士トナルモノ、往々ニコレアリ、亞爾費立〔意太利ノ詩人〕ハ、普拉打克ノ英雄傳ヲ讀ミ、コレヨリ感激シ、始テ藝文ニ從事セリ、雷閥拉〔ジエスイト一派ノ開基ノ祖〕ハ、バムペイルナ〔士班ノ一都府〕ノ圍レシ時、歩兵トナリテ戰ヒ、脚脛ニ大傷ヲ受、床ニ臥シテアリシガ、鬱悶ヲ遣ンガ爲ニ、一册ノ書ヲ借ント、傍人ニ求シニ、偶「ゼ、ライヴス、ヲフ、ゼ、セインツ」〔聖徒ノ行狀〕ヲ持シ來ル、雷閥拉コレヲ讀ミ、大ニ感發シ、コレヨリ、一敎宗ヲ創立セント、志ヲ立タリシトナリ、路楊亦コレニ類ス、甞テ偶「ライフ、エンド、ライテングス、ヲフ、ジヨン。ハス」〔潤。哈斯〔ボヒミアノ人ナリ、羅馬敎ニ抗シ、新說ヲ立シガ、異端ト名ヅケラレテ殺サル〕ノ行狀、及ビソノ遺文〕ヲ讀シガ、コレニ由テ、ソノ大事業ヲ擔任セル志ヲ發出セシト云リ、學士烏爾弗ハ、弗蘭西士維未耶ノ行狀ヲ讀ミ、コレヨリ奮勵シテ、傳法敎士トナレリ、ソノ一生ノ間、丹誠ノ心ヲ盡シ、剛烈ノ行ヲ做シハ、少年ノ時、コノ書ノ火、胸中ニ、熱傳ハリシニ由リ、維廉。加禮、マタ傳法敎士トナリ、コノ職ニ心力ヲ委ント思シハ、加比丹古克ノ航海記ヲ讀ミ、感激スルトコロアリシニ由リトナリ、
blocks.genbun: Sometimes a book containing a noble exemplar of life, taken up at random, merely with the object of reading it as a pastime, has been known to call forth energies whose existence had not before been suspected. Alfieri was first drawn with passion to literature by reading ‘Plutarch’s Lives.’ Loyola, when a soldier serving at the siege of Pampeluna, and laid up by a dangerous wound in his leg, asked for a book to divert his thoughts: the ‘Lives of the Saints’ was brought to him, and its perusal so inflamed his mind, that he determined thenceforth to devote himself to the founding of a religious order. Luther, in like manner, was inspired to undertake the great labours of his life by a perusal of the ‘Life and Writings of John Huss.’ Dr. Wolff was stimulated to enter upon his missionary career by reading the ‘Life of Francis Xavier;’ and the book fired his youthful bosom with a passion the most sincere and ardent to devote himself to the enterprise of his life. William Carey, also, got the first idea of entering upon his sublime labours as a missionary from a perusal of the Voyages of Captain Cook.

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十七　花納爾進脩ノ益ヲ得タリシ書ヲ評論ス
blocks.text: 弗蘭西士。花納爾、其日記ノ中ニ、最モ感發進脩ノ益ヲ得タリシ書名ヲ錄セリ、公鐸爾西ノ訶爾羅ニ誄スル文辭、若照。禮諾爾圖ノ理論、倍根ノ文集、培納的ノ著セル馬實。海爾ノ傳、以上四種ノ書ノ如キ、最モソノ熱好セルモノナリ、
blocks.genbun: Francis Horner was accustomed to note in his diary and letters the books by which he was most improved and influenced. Amongst these were Condorcet’s ‘Eloge of Haller,’ Sir Joshua Reynolds’ ‘Discourses,’ the writings of Bacon, and ‘Burnet’s Account of Sir Matthew Hale.’

chu.n: 原文は「日記と手紙の中に」

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 花納爾曰、海爾ノ傳、極大極奇ノ功勞ヲ描出リ、予ヲシテ感慕ニ堪ザラシム、公氏ノ誄文ヲ讀ゴトニ、心胸跳動セザルコトナシ、コレ嘆美ニ由ヤ、熱好ニ由ヤ、望ヲ失ニ由ヤ、予自ラソノ然ユヱンヲ知ズ、禮氏ノ理論、予ヲシテ深ク自脩ルノ心志ヲ激勵セシメタリ、倍根文集ヲ除ノ外、コレニ及モノナシト云リ、禮諾爾圖ハ、力查遜〔有名ノ畫家〕ノ著セル有名ナル一畫工ノ傳ヲ讀シヨリ、コレニ倣ント思ヒ起セリ、畫家海同ハ、禮氏ノ傳ヲ讀シヨリ、感激シテ畫ヲ學リ、カクノ如ク、勇氣大志アル人ノ行狀ハ、次第ニ後人ノ志氣ヲ惹起シ其ヲシテ、勉强ノ功ニ由テ、卓絕ノ名ヲ得セシムルナリ、コノ故ニ、儀範ノ鏈條ハ、ソノ長ヿ極ナク、ソノ竟トコロヲ知ズ、コレヲ觀ルモノ、嘆美ノ心ヨリ、慕倣ノ心ヲ生ジ、慕倣ノ心ヨリ、善良ノ行、妙絕ノ技、相續テ生ジ、道統ノ傳、永ク世ニ絕ザルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: The perusal of the last-mentioned book—the portrait of a prodigy of labour—Horner says, filled him with enthusiasm. Of Condorcet’s ‘Eloge of Haller,’ he said: “I never rise from the account of such men without a sort of thrilling palpitation about me, which I know not whether I should call admiration, ambition, or despair.” And speaking of the ‘Discourses’ of Sir Joshua Reynolds, he said: “Next to the writings of Bacon, there is no book which has more powerfully impelled me to self-culture. He is one of the first men of genius who has condescended to inform the world of the steps by which greatness is attained. The confidence with which he asserts the omnipotence of human labour has the effect of familiarising his reader with the idea that genius is an acquisition rather than a gift; whilst with all there is blended so naturally and eloquently the most elevated and passionate admiration of excellence, that upon the whole there is no book of a more inflammatory effect.” It is remarkable that Reynolds himself attributed his first passionate impulse towards the study of art, to reading Richardson’s account of a great painter; and Haydon was in like manner afterwards inflamed to follow the same pursuit by reading of the career of Reynolds. Thus the brave and aspiring life of one man lights a flame in the minds of others of like faculties and impulse; and where there is equally vigorous efforts like distinction and success will almost surely follow. Thus the chain of example is carried down through time in an endless succession of links,—admiration exciting imitation, and perpetuating the true aristocracy of genius.

blocks.vol: 第十二編　儀範又曰典型ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 十八　樂只君子ノ儀表
blocks.text: コヽニ、マタ少年ノ人ニ示ント欲スル最要ナルモノアリ、即チ快樂ノ心ヲ以テ、職事ヲ勤ル人ノ儀表ナリ、快樂ノ心ハ、精神ヲ鼓盪シ、妖魔ヲ逐去リ、人ヲシテ、艱難ノ事ニ逢𪜈、志氣ヲ挫ズシテソノ希望スルトコロノ事ヲ達セシム、蓋シ何等ノ職業ヲ論ゼズ、欣然トシテ樂メル人ハ、事ヲ爲スニ力アリテ、必ズソノ効驗ヲ見ルベシ、休模常ニ曰、我憂愁ノ心アル人ト爲テ、鉅萬ノ財ヲ擁センヨリハ、快樂ノ性質ヲ具ル人トナランヿコソ、望マシケレト云リ、額蘭未爾。沙伯黑奴賣買ノ事ヲ禁示スルヿニ、勉强從事シタリシ時、屢晩間ニ及ビ、ソノ同胞ノ家ニ往キ、コレト共ニ、笛ヲ吹キ、音樂ヲ合奏シ、ソノ心ヲ慰メタリ、沙伯又日曜日ノ夕ニ、罕垤爾聖樂ヲ奏スル時ニハ、太鼓ヲ擊リ、又暇時ニハ、寫意ノ畫ヲ作リシトゾ、勃古斯敦マタ樂只ナル君子ナリキ、甚ダ射獵ヲ好ミ、每ニソノ兒子輩ト、共ニ馬ニ乘リ、田野ニ往キ、ソノ他家中ニテ、兒子ト同ク種々ナル玩戲ヲ爲シトナリ、
blocks.genbun: One of the most valuable, and one of the most infectious examples which can be set before the young, is that of cheerful working. Cheerfulness gives elasticity to the spirit. Spectres fly before it; difficulties cause no despair, for they are encountered with hope, and the mind acquires that happy disposition to improve opportunities which rarely fails of success. The fervent spirit is always a healthy and happy spirit; working cheerfully itself, and stimulating others to work. It confers a dignity on even the most ordinary occupations. The most effective work, also, is usually the full-hearted work—that which passes through the hands or the head of him whose heart is glad. Hume was accustomed to say that he would rather possess a cheerful disposition—inclined always to look at the bright side of things—than with a gloomy mind to be the master of an estate of ten thousand a year. Granville Sharp, amidst his indefatigable labours on behalf of the slave, solaced himself in the evenings by taking part in glees and instrumental concerts at his brother’s house, singing, or playing on the flute, the clarionet or the oboe; and, at the Sunday evening oratorios, when Handel was played, he beat the kettle-drums. He also indulged, though sparingly, in caricature drawing. Fowell Buxton also was an eminently cheerful man; taking special pleasure in field sports, in riding about the country with his children, and in mixing in all their domestic amusements.

blocks.kotobagaki: 十九　學士亞瑙爾德ノ德行他人ヲ感化セシ事
blocks.text: 學士亞瑙爾德ハ、快樂ノ心ヲ以テ全副ノ精神ヲ出ダシ、少年ヲ敎ヘシ人ナリ、他人ノ新ニソノ居ニ至ルモノハ、忽チソノ做ベキ事業ヲ看出シ、奮勉ノ志ヲ發セザルモノナシ、コレガ門生トナレバ、忽チ課業ノ爲ベキモノアルヲ知リ、福祉ノ造ルベキモノアルヲ知リ、職分ノ盡スベキモノアルヲ見ザルモノナシ、蓋シ亞瑙爾德オモヘラク、凡百ノ學問藝術、盡ク皆用アラザルモノナク、士農工商、互ニ相資益シテ、邦國ノ利トナルヿナレバ、皆尊ビ重ズベカラザルモノナシ、此ヲ是トシ彼ヲ非トスベカラズ、我ヲ崇ビ彼ヲ卑ムベカラズ、蓋シ天地ノ間ニ、人ト生タランモノハ、必ズ天ヨリ分配セラレタル職分アリ、而シテソノ職分ヲ盡タメニ、天必ズ各ソノ才能ヲ以テ、コレニ賦予セラルヽヿナリ、故ニ何ノ事業ヲ論ゼズ、人各ソノ職分ヲ盡スハ、即チ天ニ進ム所以ノ道ナリト、蓋シ亞瑙爾德學問淵深、ソノ說謙卑ニシテ、虛驕ナラズ、公正ニシテ、偏頗ナラズ、衆異ヲ合セテ大同トナシ、民人各般ノ心力ヲ集メテ邦國一體ノ公益トナサンヿヲ欲スルモノナリ、サレバソノ門人ニ敎フルニ、天命ノ貴ブヘク、人生ノ重ンズベキヲ以テシ、職業ノ務ムベキヲ以テセリ、コレヲ聞モノ、恰モ妙香ヲ嗅ガ如ク、欣然トシテソノ肝脾ニ沁シ、終身受用ノ益トナレリ、亞氏ニ從テ學シ人ノ中ニ、闔國民人ノ利ヲ建ルモノ少カラズ、印度ニテ勇功アリシ合德遜、多年ノ後、印度ヨリソノ家ニ書ヲ寄セ、亞氏ノ事ヲ言テ曰ク、「ソノ德行ノ人ヲ感化スルヿ、甚ダ恒久ニシテ勢力アリ、余今日印度ニ在リテナホコレヲ覺ユ」ト云リ、
blocks.genbun: In another sphere of action, Dr. Arnold was a noble and a cheerful worker, throwing himself into the great business of his life, the training and teaching of young men, with his whole heart and soul. It is stated in his admirable biography, that “the most remarkable thing in the Laleham circle was the wonderful healthiness of tone which prevailed there. It was a place where a new comer at once felt that a great and earnest work was going forward. Every pupil was made to feel that there was a work for him to do; that his happiness, as well as his duty, lay in doing that work well. Hence an indescribable zest was communicated to a young man’s feeling about life; a strange joy came over him on discerning that he had the means of being useful, and thus of being happy; and a deep respect and ardent attachment sprang up towards him who had taught him thus to value life and his own self, and his work and mission in the world. All this was founded on the breadth and comprehensiveness of Arnold’s character, as well as its striking truth and reality; on the unfeigned regard he had for work of all kinds, and the sense he had of its value, both for the complex aggregate of society and the growth and protection of the individual. In all this there was no excitement; no predilection for one class of work above another; no enthusiasm for any one-sided object: but a humble, profound, and most religious consciousness that work is the appointed calling of man on earth; the end for which his various faculties were given; the element in which his nature is ordained to develop itself, and in which his progressive advance towards heaven is to lie.” Among the many valuable men trained for public life and usefulness by Arnold, was the gallant Hodson, of Hodson’s Horse, who, writing home from India, many years after, thus spoke of his revered master: “The influence he produced has been most lasting and striking in its effects. It is felt even in India; I cannot say more than that.”

chu.a: 他人ノ新ニソノ居ニ至ルモノハ

blocks.kotobagaki: 二十　潤。辛克禮ノ事
blocks.text: 潤。辛克禮ハ、該德納斯ノ大產ノ家ニ生ル、十五歲ノ時、父死シケレバ、早ク主人トナリ、家事ヲ經紀ス、十八歲ノ時ヨリ、該德納斯ノ地ヲ好情形ニ改メント志ヲ起シ、奮テコノ事ニ任ゼリ、抑モ該德納斯ハ、蘇葛蘭ノ北邊ニシテ、猛惡ノ海ニ向ヒ、田野荒蕪シ、人ノコレヲ占ルモノ少ナク、小農ノ貧キモノハ、多ハ馬ヲ畜ヿ能ズ、婦人ヲシテ擔負ノ事ヲ爲シム、サレバ、貧家ニテ、馬ヲ失フトキハ、ソノ代ニ、婦ヲ娶ルヿ、常ノ習ナリキ、マタコノ地方ニ、道路橋梁ナシ、牧人ノ畜產ヲ驅テ、南方ニ赴クモノハ、畜產ト共ニ水ニ泅キ、川ヲ渡ル、他所ヨリ該德納斯ニ至ルニ、ソノ道路、山ノ脇ニアリテ、脚下數十丈ノ深ニ、海水衝盪怒號セリ、辛克禮コノ時、年甚ダ少カリシニ、ベン。チエイルトノ山ニ、新道ヲ開ベシト、思ヒ立シカバ、鄕里ノ老人、イカデ、サル事ノ成ベキヤトテ、竊ニ嘲リ笑フ、サレドモ、辛克禮アル夏ノ日ノ曉ニ、二百人ヲ召集メ、道路ヲ治シメ、自ラコレニ先ダチ指揮シケレバ、昨日マデ辛シテ馬ヲ率テ過シ危險ナル六里ノ路、忽チ車輪ヲ轉ズベクゾナリニケル、不思議ト云モ愚ナリ、コレヨリ其他、所々ノ道路ヲ造リ、橋ヲ架シ、水磨ヲ作リ、廢地ヲ開墾シ、耕種ノ良法ヲ用ヒ、穀物ノ運輸ヲ整理シ、又稼穡ヲ勉ルモノニハ、賞銀ヲ給與シテ、人民ノ精神ヲ振起セシカバ、該德納斯道路ノ治レル、耕田捕魚ノ盛ナルヿ、近郡ニ師法トセラルヽニ至レリ、辛克禮ノ少キ時、コノ地ヨリ驛信ヲ發スル、週七日、只一回ニテ、一人ノ快差コレヲ擔ヘ徃ルノミ、辛氏曰ク、我驛車ノ托爾索ニ至ルヿヲ見ザルウチハ、決シテ休息セザルベシトイヘド、鄕里ノ人、コレヲ信ズルモノナク、凡ソ能スベカラザル情事ニ逢ヘバ、相語リテ曰ク、辛君每日驛車ノ托爾索ニ至ルヲ見ントキニコソ、コレ亦成就スベケレトゾ云ケリ、然ニ辛氏遂ニ生時ニ及ビ、ソノ事ノ成ルヲ見タリ、
blocks.genbun: The useful influence which a right-hearted man of energy and industry may exercise amongst his neighbours and dependants, and accomplish for his country, cannot, perhaps, be better illustrated than by the career of Sir John Sinclair; characterized by the Abbé Gregoire as “the most indefatigable man in Europe.” He was originally a country laird, born to a considerable estate situated near John o’ Groat’s House, almost beyond the beat of civilization, in a bare wild country fronting the stormy North Sea. His father dying while he was a youth of sixteen, the management of the family property thus early devolved upon him; and at eighteen he began a course of vigorous improvement in the county of Caithness, which eventually spread all over Scotland. Agriculture then was in a most backward state; the fields were unenclosed, the lands undrained; the small farmers of Caithness were so poor that they could scarcely afford to keep a horse or shelty; the hard work was chiefly done, and the burdens borne, by the women; and if a cottier lost a horse it was not unusual for him to marry a wife as the cheapest substitute. The country was without roads or bridges; and drovers driving their cattle south had to swim the rivers along with their beasts. The chief track leading into Caithness lay along a high shelf on a mountain side, the road being some hundred feet of clear perpendicular height above the sea which dashed below. Sir John, though a mere youth, determined to make a new road over the hill of Ben Cheilt, the old let-alone proprietors, however, regarding his scheme with incredulity and derision. But he himself laid out the road, assembled some twelve hundred workmen early one summer’s morning, set them simultaneously to work, superintending their labours, and stimulating them by his presence and example; and before night, what had been a dangerous sheep track, six miles in length, hardly passable for led horses, was made practicable for wheel-carriages as if by the power of magic. It was an admirable example of energy and well-directed labour, which could not fail to have a most salutary influence upon the surrounding population. He then proceeded to make more roads, to erect mills, to build bridges, and to enclose and cultivate the waste lands. He introduced improved methods of culture, and regular rotation of crops, distributing small premiums to encourage industry; and he thus soon quickened the whole frame of society within reach of his influence, and infused an entirely new spirit into the cultivators of the soil. From being one of the most inaccessible districts of the north—the very ultima Thule of civilization—Caithness became a pattern county for its roads, its agriculture, and its fisheries. In Sinclair’s youth, the post was carried by a runner only once a week, and the young baronet then declared that he would never rest till a coach drove daily to Thurso. The people of the neighbourhood could not believe in any such thing, and it became a proverb in the county to say of an utterly impossible scheme, “Ou, ay, that will come to pass when Sir John sees the daily mail at Thurso!” But Sir John lived to see his dream realized, and the daily mail established to Thurso.

blocks.text: 英國ノ綿羊毛、交易塲ニテ重ゼラレシモノ、次第ニ衰ヘ惡クナリシカバ、辛克禮コレヲ修メ善セント思ヒ、コレガ爲ニ綿羊會社ヲ立設ケ、自己ノ費用ヲ以テ、諸方ヨリ、羊八百ヲ輸入シ、畜牧ノ事ヲ經紀セリ、本地ノ牧人、始メ南方ノ良種、北地ニ蕃育スベカラズト思ヒ、辛氏ノ爲トコロヲ侮ドリシガ、辛氏耐性ニ由テ、數年ノ後、北方四郡ヨリ產スル南種ノ綿羊、三十萬ノ大數ニ至ル、コノ時ヨリ以前、蘇國人民ノ產業甚ダ非薄ナリシモノ、コレニ由テ貨財大イニ生殖スルヲ得タリ、
blocks.genbun: The circle of his benevolent operation gradually widened. Observing the serious deterioration which had taken place in the quality of British wool,—one of the staple commodities of the country,—he forthwith, though but a private and little-known country gentleman, devoted himself to its improvement. By his personal exertions he established the British Wool Society for the purpose, and himself led the way to practical improvement by importing 800 sheep from all countries, at his own expense. The result was, the introduction into Scotland of the celebrated Cheviot breed. Sheep farmers scouted the idea of south country flocks being able to thrive in the far north. But Sir John persevered; and in a few years there were not fewer than 300,000 Cheviots diffused over the four northern counties alone. The value of all grazing land was thus enormously increased; and Scotch estates, which before were comparatively worthless, began to yield large rentals.

blocks.text: 既ニシテ辛克禮、該德納斯ノ民衆ニ撰バレ、巴力門議士ノ員ニ列スルヿ、凡ソ三十年、ソノ間、機會ヲ失ズシテ、有用ノ務ニ從事シ、功勞ヲ積タリ、首輔比的、深ク辛氏ノ力ヲ國事ニ竭セルヲ重シ、一日ソノ家ヲ訪ヒ、何事ナリトモ、ソノ欲スルトコロノモノ、助マヰラスベシトイフ、他人ナラバ、或ハ自己ノ顯達ヲモ望ムベキニ、辛氏、答テ、サラバ、國中ノ農事ヲ勵サン爲ニ、司農會所ヲ建ルヿニ力ヲ添玉ヘト云リ、阿他爾。雍、コノ事、成リ難カルベシト思ヒ、或時辛氏ニ向ヒ、足下ノ司農會所ハ、月球ノ中ニアルベシト云シガ、辛氏首トシテ、コノ事ヲ唱ヘ、衆人ヲシテ、コヽニ著意セシメ、巴力門議士ヲシテ、大半ソノ說ニ同ゼシメタレバ、遂ニ司農會所、建ヿヲ得、辛氏ソノ監督トナル、コレニ由リ、國人、農事ニ勸ミ、本錢ヲ出スモノ多ク、幾何モナク、不列顚合邦ノ中、田地開墾スルモノ數萬畆ニ及ベリ、辛氏マタ漁事ヲ勸メ、力ヲ盡ス、今托爾索威克ニ於テ、捕魚ノ盛ンナル、天下コレニ比スルモノナキハ偏ニ辛氏ノ功ナリ、
blocks.genbun: Returned by Caithness to Parliament, in which he remained for thirty years, rarely missing a division, his position gave him farther opportunities of usefulness, which he did not neglect to employ. Mr. Pitt, observing his persevering energy in all useful public projects, sent for him to Downing Street, and voluntarily proposed his assistance in any object he might have in view. Another man might have thought of himself and his own promotion; but Sir John characteristically replied, that he desired no favour for himself, but intimated that the reward most gratifying to his feelings would be Mr. Pitt’s assistance in the establishment of a National Board of Agriculture. Arthur Young laid a bet with the baronet that his scheme would never be established, adding, “Your Board of Agriculture will be in the moon!” But vigorously setting to work, he roused public attention to the subject, enlisted a majority of Parliament on his side, and eventually established the Board, of which he was appointed President. The result of its action need not be described, but the stimulus which it gave to agriculture and stock-raising was shortly felt throughout the whole United Kingdom, and tens of thousands of acres were redeemed from barrenness by its operation. He was equally indefatigable in encouraging the establishment of fisheries; and the successful founding of these great branches of British industry at Thurso and Wick was mainly due to his exertions. He urged for long years, and at length succeeded in obtaining the enclosure of a harbour for the latter place, which is perhaps the greatest and most prosperous fishing town in the world.

blocks.genbun: Sir John threw his personal energy into every work in which he engaged, rousing the inert, stimulating the idle, encouraging the hopeful, and working with all. When a French invasion was threatened, he offered to Mr. Pitt to raise a regiment on his own estate, and he was as good as his word. He went down to the north, and raised a battalion of 600 men, afterwards increased to 1000; and it was admitted to be one of the finest volunteer regiments ever raised, inspired throughout by his own noble and patriotic spirit. While commanding officer of the camp at Aberdeen he held the offices of a Director of the Bank of Scotland, Chairman of the British Wool Society, Provost of Wick, Director of the British Fishery Society, Commissioner for issuing Exchequer Bills, Member of Parliament for Caithness, and President of the Board of Agriculture. Amidst all this multifarious and self-imposed work, he even found time to write books, enough of themselves to establish a reputation. When Mr. Rush, the American Ambassador, arrived in England, he relates that he inquired of Mr. Coke of Holkham, what was the best work on Agriculture, and was referred to Sir John Sinclair’s; and when he further asked of Mr. Vansittart, Chancellor of the Exchequer, what was the best work on British Finance, he was again referred to a work by Sir John Sinclair, his ‘History of the Public Revenue.’ But the great monument of his indefatigable industry, a work that would have appalled other men, but only served to rouse and sustain his energy, was his ‘Statistical Account of Scotland,’ in twenty-one volumes, one of the most valuable practical works ever published in any age or country. Amid a host of other pursuits it occupied him nearly eight years of hard labour, during which he received, and attended to, upwards of 20,000 letters on the subject. It was a thoroughly patriotic undertaking, from which he derived no personal advantage whatever, beyond the honour of having completed it. The whole of the profits were assigned by him to the Society for the Sons of the Clergy in Scotland. The publication of the book led to great public improvements; it was followed by the immediate abolition of several oppressive feudal rights, to which it called attention; the salaries of schoolmasters and clergymen in many parishes were increased; and an increased stimulus was given to agriculture throughout Scotland. Sir John then publicly offered to undertake the much greater labour of collecting and publishing a similar Statistical Account of England; but unhappily the then Archbishop of Canterbury refused to sanction it, lest it should interfere with the tithes of the clergy, and the idea was abandoned.

blocks.genbun: A remarkable illustration of his energetic promptitude was the manner in which he once provided, on a great emergency, for the relief of the manufacturing districts. In 1793 the stagnation produced by the war led to an unusual number of bankruptcies, and many of the first houses in Manchester and Glasgow were tottering, not so much from want of property, but because the usual sources of trade and credit were for the time closed up. A period of intense distress amongst the labouring classes seemed imminent, when Sir John urged, in Parliament, that Exchequer notes to the amount of five millions should be issued immediately as a loan to such merchants as could give security. This suggestion was adopted, and his offer to carry out his plan, in conjunction with certain members named by him, was also accepted. The vote was passed late at night, and early next morning Sir John, anticipating the delays of officialism and red tape, proceeded to bankers in the city, and borrowed of them, on his own personal security, the sum of 70,000l., which he despatched the same evening to those merchants who were in the most urgent need of assistance. Pitt meeting Sir John in the House, expressed his great regret that the pressing wants of Manchester and Glasgow could not be supplied so soon as was desirable, adding, “The money cannot be raised for some days.” “It is already gone! it left London by to-night’s mail!” was Sir John’s triumphant reply; and in afterwards relating the anecdote he added, with a smile of pleasure, “Pitt was as much startled as if I had stabbed him.” To the last this great, good man worked on usefully and cheerfully, setting a great example for his family and for his country. In so laboriously seeking others’ good, it might be said that he found his own—not wealth, for his generosity seriously impaired his private fortune, but happiness, and self-satisfaction, and the peace that passes knowledge. A great patriot, with magnificent powers of work, he nobly did his duty to his country; yet he was not neglectful of his own household and home. His sons and daughters grew up to honour and usefulness; and it was one of the proudest things Sir John could say, when verging on his eightieth year, that he had lived to see seven sons grown up, not one of whom had incurred a debt he could not pay, or caused him a sorrow that could have been avoided.

“For who can always act? but he, To whom a thousand memories call, Not being less but more than all The gentleness he seemed to be,
But seemed the thing he was, and joined Each office of the social hour To noble manners, as the flower And native growth of noble mind;
And thus he bore without abuse The grand old name of Gentleman.”—Tennyson.
“Es bildet ein Talent sich in der Stille, Sich ein Charakter in dem Strom der Welt.”—Goethe.
“That which raises a country, that which strengthens a country, and that which dignifies a country,—that which spreads her power, creates her moral influence, and makes her respected and submitted to, bends the hearts of millions, and bows down the pride of nations to her—the instrument of obedience, the fountain of supremacy, the true throne, crown, and sceptre of a nation;—this aristocracy is not an aristocracy of blood, not an aristocracy of fashion, not an aristocracy of talent only; it is an aristocracy of Character. That is the true heraldry of man.”—The Times.

chu.n: 原書はこの前に、テニソンの詩（段落 1〜3）とゲーテの言葉（段落 4）を題辞として置く。中村が訳したのは『タイムズ』の一節（段落 5）だけである
原文は「流行の貴族でもなく」

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 一　品行ハ人ノ有ル最貴ナル物
blocks.text: 人ノ斯世ニアル、眞正ノ權勢ト稱スベキモノハ、品行ナリ、品行ハ、爵位ヲ假ズシテ、自ラ爵位ヲ具ヘ、財貨ヲ擁セズシテ、別ニ產業ヲ有リ、何ナル地位ニ居ル𪜈、ソノ地位ヲシテ榮光アラシメ、何ナル會社ニ入ル𪜈、ソノ會社ヲシテ、崇高ナラシメ、ソノ大勢力アルヿ、貨財ノ及ブベキニ非ズ、他人ヨリ尊敬セラレテ、コレヲ妬忌スルモノナシ、言語ナクシテ、他人ヲ感化スルヿ、常ニ言語スルガ如シ、蓋シ品行ノ善ナルモノハ、篤敬正直ニシテ、事ヲ處スル、必ズソノ宜ニ合フニ在リ、而シテソノ他人ノ信任ヲ得、他人ノ敬重ヲ得ルヿ、天下ニ比スベキモノアラズ、
blocks.genbun: THE crown and glory of life is Character. It is the noblest possession of a man, constituting a rank in itself, and an estate in the general goodwill; dignifying every station, and exalting every position in society. It exercises a greater power than wealth, and secures all the honour without the jealousies of fame. It carries with it an influence which always tells; for it is the result of proved honour, rectitude, and consistency—qualities which, perhaps more than any other, command the general confidence and respect of mankind.

chu.a: 言語ナクシテ、他人ヲ感化スルヿ、常ニ言語スルガ如シ
chu.n: 原文は「それは、いつでも効き目のある感化力をともなう」

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 品行ノ善ナルモノハ、人性ヨリ發スル形狀ノ善ナルモノナリ、マタ各人ニ具ハル天命ト、一致スルモノナリ、故ニ品行ノ善ナル人ハ、衆人天良是非ノ心ニ合ノミナラズ、邦國ノ善ク治マレル動機ノ本ナリ、コレ平世ノミニ限ズ、戰鬪ノ時ト雖𪜈、亦然リ、故ニ拿破崙戰ヲ論ジテ、德善ノ勢力ハ、身體ノ勢力ニ十倍スト云リ、抑モ邦國ノ勢力トイヒ、邦國ノ農工繁盛トイヒ、邦國ノ文化昌明ト云モノ、悉ク皆人民各箇ノ品行ニ關係スルヿナリ、而シテ律法トイヒ、制度ト云モノモ、特ニ人民ノ品行ヨリ、漸々ニ生長シテ、形ヲ成セルモノニ外ナラズ、故ニ人民各箇ノ輕重ト、邦國一體ノ經重ト、ソノ斤兩適ニ相同シ、人類ノ尊卑コソ、實ハ邦國ノ尊卑ナレ、凡ソ事原因アレバ、必ズソノ效驗アリ、故ニ人民ノ品行ハ、邦國百事ノ原因ナレバ、ソノ品行ノ善惡ニ隨ヒテ、ソノ善惡ノ效驗ヲ邦國ノ景象ニ發スルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: Character is human nature in its best form. It is moral order embodied in the individual. Men of character are not only the conscience of society, but in every well-governed State they are its best motive power; for it is moral qualities in the main which rule the world. Even in war, Napoleon said the moral is to the physical as ten to one. The strength, the industry, and the civilisation of nations—all depend upon individual character; and the very foundations of civil security rest upon it. Laws and institutions are but its outgrowth. In the just balance of nature, individuals, nations, and races, will obtain just so much as they deserve, and no more. And as effect finds its cause, so surely does quality of character amongst a people produce its befitting results.

chu.a: 故ニ人民各箇ノ輕重ト
chu.n: 原文は「自然の正しいはかりにかけられて、個人も、国民も、民族も、ちょうど自分に値するだけのものを得るのであり、それより多くは得ない」。また、原文にある「世界を治めるのは、おもに道徳上の性質だからである」「市民の安全の土台そのものも、その上にのっている」は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 二　加寧、拉設爾ノ嘉言、花納爾ノ善行、
blocks.text: 人タトヒ學識少ク、才能乏ク、而シテ又貲產多カラズト雖𪜈、尙モソノ品行極善ナレバ、ソノ地位ヲ論セズ、或ハ工塲ニ在𪜈、或ハ市井ニ在𪜈、或ハ議政會所ニ在𪜈、必ズソノ感化自ラ他人ニ及ブベシ、加寧ハ、英王若爾日第三ノ時ノ宰輔ナリ、一千八百零一年、ソノ志ヲ言テ曰、吾ガ進ミ行クベキノ道路ハ、品行ニ由リテ勢位ニ進ムベキノミ、予思フニ、コノ道路ハ、捷速ナラズ、然𪜈鞏固安穩ナルモノハ、コレニ如モノナシト云リ、試ニ思ヘ、誰ニテモ、才智ノ人ヲ、嘆美賞譽スベケレ𪜈、必シモコノ人ニ信任倚賴セザルベシ、然トキハ、人ニハ必ズ才智ヨリ要重ナルモノヽアリテ存スルヿヲ知ルベシ、潤。拉設爾嘗テ曰、才智アル人ニ、輔助ヲ求レ𪜈、必ズ品行アル人ノ指導ニ隨ガフ、コレ英人ノ性ナリト云ルハ、眞確ノ言ト爲ベシ、
blocks.genbun: Though a man have comparatively little culture, slender abilities, and but small wealth, yet, if his character be of sterling worth, he will always command an influence, whether it be in the workshop, the counting-house, the mart, or the senate. Canning wisely wrote in 1801, “My road must be through Character to power; I will try no other course; and I am sanguine enough to believe that this course, though not perhaps the quickest, is the surest.” You may admire men of intellect; but something more is necessary before you will trust them. Hence Lord John Russell once observed in a sentence full of truth, “It is the nature of party in England to ask the assistance of men of genius, but to follow the guidance of men of character.”

chu.a: 加寧ハ、英王若爾日第三ノ時ノ宰輔ナリ
chu.n: カニングの説明は中村が加えたもの。原文にある「ほかの道は試すまい」は、中村の訳にはない
原文は「会計事務所であれ、市場であれ」
原文は「これがイギリスの党派というものの性質である」

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 近世弗蘭西士。花納爾ノ行狀、實ニコノ論ノ謬ザルヲ明ニ足リ、西德尼。斯密士、嘗テ花納爾ヲ評シテ、神命十誡ヲソノ面上ニ印スルガ如シト云リ、勞爾德格克畔、コレヲ評シテ曰ク、花納爾ノ履歷ハ、少年ノ心正キモノ、コレヲ聞テ感化セザルモノ、百ニ一モアラズ、誠ニ貴重スルニ堪タリ、マタ奇特ナルニ驚クベシ、花氏僅ニ三十八歲ニシテ沒セリ、ソノ衆人ニ敬愛セラルヽヿ、特ニ深ク、信服セラルヽヿ、甚ダ大ナリ、死スル時、心情ナキ人、及穢行アル人ヲ除ノ外、闔國悲哀哭泣セザルモノナシ、巴力門議院ニ於テ、死亡セル官員ヲ恭敬セシヿ、コノ時ヨリ甚モノナシ、予因テ天下年少ノ人ニ問ント欲ス、花氏何ヲ以テ、コレヲ得タルヤ、世爵ヲ以テノ故カト云バ、花氏ハ壹丁不ニ住ル商人ノ子ナリ、財貨ヲ以テノ故カト云バ、花氏及ビソノ親族、嘗テ餘ル銀錢一箇ヲ有ズ、官職ヲ以ノ故カト云バ、花氏權威アラザル小祿ノ官員ニ過ズ、而モ僅數年コレニ居ルノミ、才能ヲ以ノ故カト云バ、花氏中等ノ資性ニシテ、英才ノ彰著セルモノナク、特ニ小心謹愼ニシテ、事ヲ作ス遲緩ナルノミ、ソノ志唯心ニ是ト許ストコロノモノヲ爲ルノミ、辯才ヲ以ノ故カト云バ、花氏ハ、辯論ノ士ノ或ハ人ヲ驚嚇シ、或ハ人ヲ挑唆スル如キヿナシ、ソノ說話穩靜ニシテ、滋味アルノミ、容貌ノ美雅ナルモノアリテ、人心ヲ醺醉スルカト云ニ、花氏特ニ正直ニシテ和順ナルノミ、然バ何ヲ以テコレヲ得タルヤ、蓋シ花氏ハ良善ノ本領、良善ノ心情アリテ、敬愼ニシテ、職事ヲ勤ムル人ナリ、特ニコノ品行アルノ故ニ由リテ、コレニ就キコレト交ルモノヲシテ、觀感信服セシメ、一世ヲ傾動スルニ至リ、コノ品行ハ、別ニ天稟ノ才ヲ要セズ、他人ノ助ヲ要セズ、人々自己ニ修得ラルベキモノナリ、然バ花氏極テ平常ナル品行ヲ己ニ修メ、極テ奇特ナル感化ヲ世ニ施セシト云フベシ、抑モコノ時ニ當テ、百姓會所ノ中ソノ才能智辯、花氏ニ百倍スルモノ少カラズ、然𪜈德行ノ價ヲ論ズレバ、花氏遠クコレニ超過セリ、誠ニソノ生平ヲ觀ルトキハ、苟モ能善行ヲ修レバ、才氣中人ニ踰ズト雖𪜈、一世ノ表率トナルヿヲ得ベク、才能智辯ヲ競ヘル世ト雖𪜈、他人ノ敬愛ヲ得ベキヲ知ベシ、
notes: *（欄外頭注、神命十誡の小字四行。判読できず〓）
blocks.genbun: This was strikingly illustrated in the career of the late Francis Horner—a man of whom Sydney Smith said that the Ten Commandments were stamped upon his countenance. “The valuable and peculiar light,” says Lord Cockburn, “in which his history is calculated to inspire every right-minded youth, is this. He died at the age of thirty-eight; possessed of greater public influence than any other private man; and admired, beloved, trusted, and deplored by all, except the heartless or the base. No greater homage was ever paid in Parliament to any deceased member. Now let every young man ask—how was this attained? By rank? He was the son of an Edinburgh merchant. By wealth? Neither he, nor any of his relations, ever had a superfluous sixpence. By office? He held but one, and only for a few years, of no influence, and with very little pay. By talents? His were not splendid, and he had no genius. Cautious and slow, his only ambition was to be right. By eloquence? He spoke in calm, good taste, without any of the oratory that either terrifies or seduces. By any fascination of manner? His was only correct and agreeable. By what, then, was it? Merely by sense, industry, good principles, and a good heart—qualities which no well-constituted mind need ever despair of attaining. It was the force of his character that raised him; and this character not impressed upon him by nature, but formed, out of no peculiarly fine elements, by himself. There were many in the House of Commons of far greater ability and eloquence. But no one surpassed him in the combination of an adequate portion of these with moral worth. Horner was born to show what moderate powers, unaided by anything whatever except culture and goodness, may achieve, even when these powers are displayed amidst the competition and jealousy of public life.”

chu.a: 嘗テ餘ル銀錢一箇ヲ有ズ
chu.n: 原文は「余分な六ペンス貨一枚持ったことがなかった」
原文は House of Commons（下院）

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 三　富蘭克林、孟典ノ事
blocks.text: 富蘭克林ハ、亞米利加ノ慷慨義烈ノ士ニシテ、亦理學者ナリ、崇高ノ職ニ居リ、國ニ勳勞アリシガ、常ニ自ラソノ功績ヲ成タルヿヲ、才能智辯ニ歸セズシテ、ソノ品行ノ信實ナルヿニ歸セリ、故ニソノ言ニ曰ク、予タヾ品行信實ナルヲ以テ、吾國人ニ重ゼラレタリ、予言語拙惡ニシテ、一句ヲ道出ニモ、多少ノ揀擇ヲ費セリ、然𪜈吾志願スルトコロノモノハ、常ニ能行ルヽヿヲ得タリト云リ、蓋シ品行能他人ノ信任ヲ得ルヿ、尊卑上下ノ別アラズ、サレバ魯西亞ノ帝亞力山大ハ、人コレヲ評シテ、ソノ一身ノ品行、適ニソノ國法ト價値相當ルト云リ、孟典ハ、法國ノ文行衆ニ顯レシ人ナリ、法國內亂アリテ、兩黨相戰シ時、紳董ノ中、獨リ孟典ソノ門ヲ鎖サザリシトゾ、論者コレヲ贊シテ、孟氏一身ノ品行ソノ危難ヲ防クニ足ルヿ、遙カニ一隊ノ兵馬ヨリ勝レリト云リ、
blocks.genbun: Franklin, also, attributed his success as a public man, not to his talents or his powers of speaking—for these were but moderate—but to his known integrity of character. Hence it was, he says, “that I had so much weight with my fellow citizens. I was but a bad speaker, never eloquent, subject to much hesitation in my choice of words, hardly correct in language, and yet I generally carried my point.” Character creates confidence in men in high station as well as in humble life. It was said of the first Emperor Alexander of Russia, that his personal character was equivalent to a constitution. During the wars of the Fronde, Montaigne was the only man amongst the French gentry who kept his castle gates unbarred; and it was said of him, that his personal character was a better protection for him than a regiment of horse would have been.

chu.a: 富蘭克林ハ、亞米利加ノ慷慨義烈ノ士ニシテ
chu.n: フランクリンの人物の説明（「國ニ勳勞アリシガ」まで）は中村が加えたもの。原文にある「それらはほどほどのものにすぎなかった」「けっして雄弁ではなく」「言葉づかいもほとんど正しくなかった」は、中村の訳にはない
原文は「ロシアの皇帝アレクサンドル一世」。「國法」は、原文では constitution（憲法）

chu.a: 法國內亂アリテ、兩黨相戰シ時
chu.n: 原文は「フロンドの乱のあいだ」。「孟典ハ、法國ノ文行衆ニ顯レシ人ナリ」は中村が加えた説明。なおフロンドの乱（一六四八〜五三年）はモンテーニュ（一五九二年没）の死後のことで、モンテーニュが門を閉ざさなかったのは、十六世紀の宗教戦争のときである
原文は「一個連隊の騎兵」

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 四　品行ハ勢力ナリ
blocks.text: 希臘ノ古諺ニ、智識ハ勢力ナリト云𪜈、品行ハ勢力ナリト曰ヿノ意義、更ニ好ニ如ズ、天良ヲ失ヘル知覺ノ心、品行ナキノ才智、善良ナラザルノ伶俐ハ、各ソノ分ニ隨ヒ、權能勢力ナシト云ベカラズ、然𪜈、畢竟欺詐刁惡ヲ作タメノ勢力ノミ、故ニ賤ムベクシテ稱スルニ足ス、譬ハ剪徑賊及ビ攫客ノ姦巧ヲ用ヒテ他人ノ物ヲ攘奪スルガ如シ、ソノ巧妙ヲ稱贊スルヲ得ベクンヤ、
blocks.genbun: That character is power, is true in a much higher sense than that knowledge is power. Mind without heart, intelligence without conduct, cleverness without goodness, are powers in their way, but they may be powers only for mischief. We may be instructed or amused by them; but it is sometimes as difficult to admire them as it would be to admire the dexterity of a pickpocket or the horsemanship of a highwayman.

chu.n: 「ギリシアの古いことわざ」は中村が加えたもの。原文は「知識は力である」とだけ言う。原文にある「私たちはそれらから教えられたり、楽しまされたりすることはあるだろう」は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 人ノ品行ハ、眞實善良ノ德アルヲ以テ本ト爲ス、コノ德アリテ、又心志ノ力アリ、二者合テ一トナレバ、ソノ勢力ノ强ヿ、天下コレヲ禦モノナカルベシ、カクノ如キノ人ハ、善ヲ作ニ勇ミ、惡ヲ防ニ强ク、艱難ヲ忍ビ、凶禍ニ敵スルノ力アルヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: Truthfulness, integrity, and goodness—qualities that hang not on any man’s breath—form the essence of manly character, or, as one of our old writers has it, “that inbred loyalty unto Virtue which can serve her without a livery.” He who possesses these qualities, united with strength of purpose, carries with him a power which is irresistible. He is strong to do good, strong to resist evil, and strong to bear up under difficulty and misfortune.

chu.a: 人ノ品行ハ、眞實善良ノ德アルヲ以テ本ト爲ス
chu.n: 原文にある「だれの口先にも左右されない」と、昔の著述家の言葉（「お仕着せなしに徳に仕えることのできる、生まれながらの徳への忠誠」）は、中村の訳にはない

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.text: 格倫納ノ士提反、鄙賤ナル仇敵ノ手ニ落シ時、敵人コレヲ嘲笑シテ、今汝ノ城ハ安在ヤト曰ケレバ、士提反ソノ手ヲ心上ニ當テ、コヽニ在リ」ト、毅然トシテ答シトイヘリ、品行端正ナル人ハ、凶禍災阨ニ逢トキハ、ソノ光輝益大イニ發越シ、或ハ盡ク失敗喪亡ニ至ト雖𪜈、ソノ義勇ハ却テ益大ニ顯出ヿナリ、
blocks.genbun: When Stephen of Colonna fell into the hands of his base assailants, and they asked him in derision, “Where is now your fortress?” “Here,” was his bold reply, placing his hand upon his heart. It is in misfortune that the character of the upright man shines forth with the greatest lustre; and when all else fails, he takes stand upon his integrity and his courage.

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 五　勞爾德亞斯金ノ行規
blocks.text: 勞爾德亞斯金ハ、自主ノ道理ニ原ヅキ、實事是ヲ求ムルノ人ナリ、ソノ定タリシ行狀ノ規則ハ、凡少年ノ人、コレヲ心肝ニ銘ズベシ、曰予幼年ノ時、始テ吾父ヨリ一ノ訓戒ヲ聞リ、曰常ニ自知ノ良心ニテ、コレハ己ガ職分ナリト思フコトハ、何事ニテモ、心ヲ盡シテ、之ヲ做ベク、而シテソノ成敗ハ、上帝ニ聽スベシトナリ、予コノ訓戒ヲ服膺シテ忘ズ、棺ヲ蓋ニ至マデ、コレヲ行ント欲ス、蓋今日ニ至マデ、コレヲ謹ミ守シガ、塵世ノ凶害ヲ受ザルノミナラズ、福利荐臻ヿヲ覺エタリ、實ニコノ訓戒ハ、人ノ福祉ニ至ルベキノ路ナリ、予マタコノ路ヲ兒子輩ニ指示シ、コレニ循ヒ行シメント思リ、
blocks.genbun: The rules of conduct followed by Lord Erskine—a man of sterling independence of principle and scrupulous adherence to truth—are worthy of being engraven on every young man’s heart. “It was a first command and counsel of my earliest youth,” he said, “always to do what my conscience told me to be a duty, and to leave the consequence to God. I shall carry with me the memory, and I trust the practice, of this parental lesson to the grave. I have hitherto followed it, and I have no reason to complain that my obedience to it has been a temporal sacrifice. I have found it, on the contrary, the road to prosperity and wealth, and I shall point out the same path to my children for their pursuit.”

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 六　人皆品行ヲ修善スルヿヲ以テ目的ト爲ベシ
blocks.text: 凡ソ人、ソノ品行ヲ砥礪シ、善人君子トナラント思ヒ、高尙ナル志願ヲ立ベシ、蓋シ眞善ノ品行ヲ己ニ得ント欲セバ、必ズ奮勉シテ力ヲ出スベク、ソノ德行ノ進ムニ隨ヒ、ソノ志念益堅カルベシ、抑モ人高尙ナル品行ヲ以テ、目的ト爲コトハ、甚ダ好シ、縱ヒ全ク未ダコレヲ己ニ得ルヿ能ズ𪜈、早ク已ニ邪惡ノ道ニ入ルヿヲ免カルヽナリ、垤士禮立曰、少年ノ高キヲ仰ガザルモノハ、必ラズ卑キニ俯ス、而シテ精神意氣ノ天ニ冲飛セザルモノハ、必ズ地ニ匍匐スト云リ、若爾日。花伯的ノ詩ニ曰ク、汝ノ容止ヲ卑シ、汝ノ志謀ヲ高クセヨ、然バ汝謙心ニシテ大量アルノ人ト爲ヘシ、汝ノ精神意氣ヲシテ、低沈セシムルヿ勿レ、蓋シ蒼穹ヲ目的トナシテ、箭ヲ射モノハ、一樹ヲ正鵠トスルモノニ比スレバ、遙ニ高ク戾ルベシ、蘇格蘭人ノ諺ニ曰、汝金袍ヲ掣ベシ、然バ汝ソノ一袖ヲ得ン」ト、凡ソ人、高尙ナル心術行狀ヲ、己ニ得ント志タランニハ、必ズ始發程セシ處ヨリ、遙ニ高處ニ進ベシ、縱ソノ得ルトコロノ造詣、始志セシ境地ニ及バズトモ、畢竟ソノ利益アルヿ、永ク窮リ盡ザルベシ、
blocks.genbun:
Every man is bound to aim at the possession of a good character as one of the highest objects of life. The very effort to secure it by worthy means will furnish him with a motive for exertion; and his idea of manhood, in proportion as it is elevated, will steady and animate his motive. It is well to have a high standard of life, even though we may not be able altogether to realize it. “The youth,” says Mr. Disraeli, “who does not look up will look down; and the spirit that does not soar is destined perhaps to grovel.” George Herbert wisely writes,
“Pitch thy behaviour low, thy projects high, So shall thou humble and magnanimous be. Sink not in spirit; who aimeth at the sky Shoots higher much than he that means a tree.”
He who has a high standard of living and thinking will certainly do better than he who has none at all. “Pluck at a gown of gold,” says the Scotch proverb, “and you may get a sleeve o’t.” Whoever tries for the highest results cannot fail to reach a point far in advance of that from which he started; and though the end attained may fall short of that proposed, still, the very effort to rise, of itself cannot fail to prove permanently beneficial.

chu.a: 若爾日。花伯的ノ詩ニ曰ク

blocks.vol: 第十三編　品行ヲ論ズ即眞正ノ君子ヲ論ズ
blocks.kotobagaki: 七　美名ノ價
blocks.text: 世ニ僞德僞行ノ人、マヽ少カラズ、然𪜈眞實ノ品行ハ、決シテ他人ニ誤マリ認メラルベカラズ、貨物ノ價ハ、或ハソノ眞ヲ掩ヒ、人ヲ欺クベケレ𪜈、品行ノ價ハ、シカラズ、必ズ衆人ノ眼ヲ逃レザルナリ、參將查的律斯、一箇ノ忠直ナル人ニ向ヒ、我一千金ヲ以テ、子ノ美名ヲ買ント欲スト云フ、ソノ人、何ノ故ゾト問バ、查氏戲ムレ答テ、我ハコレヲ以テ、一萬金ニ做得ベシト思ガ故ナリト、云シトナリ、
blocks.genbun: There are many counterfeits of character, but the genuine article is difficult to be mistaken. Some, knowing its money value, would assume its disguise for the purpose of imposing upon the unwary. Colonel Charteris said to a man distinguished for his honesty, “I would give a thousand pounds for your good name.” “Why?” “Because I could make ten thousand by it,” was the knave’s reply.
